#3970. "There is no excuse for what I did," Nvidia CEO says, as affair with an alleged Chinese spy makes the US-China AI race look even more ridiculous

Just saying, Jensen, this probably doesn't happen if you stick to gaming GPUs

Ostensible graphics card company and definite AI giants Nvidia have commissioned an independent investigation into themselves, amid reports that CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Per both the New York Times and Nvidia themselves, Nvidia offered to go under the microscope after US intelligence organisations elected to investigate Huang’s paramour, Chinese national Alice Huang (no, uh, relation, and also known as Huang Le), on suspicion of sharing sensitive information with Beijing. The Nvidia-running, leather-jacketed Huang has thus far only copped to an unspecified affair, admitting in an extraordinary public statement that he was "unfaithful to my wife." Still, the two investigations are likely to start a bizarre new leg in the alread-messy AI arms race that the US and China have been indulging in for years.

See, the basis for Huang and Huang’s relationship appears to be the same thing that’s been fucking us as PC owners: data centres and AI hardware. Alice Huang is a former managing director of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company who’ve bought billions of US dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips – and have been investigated for allegedly getting some of them into the hands of Chinese companies, in defiance of US trade restrictions on goods that might threaten the States’ AI dominance. Possibly also, given both countries’ increasing interest in the technology’s military uses, their perception of national security.

Many of these embargo-dodging accusations originate from after Alice Huang left Megaspeed, though she is now under that separate investigation for intelligence-sharing, and the prospect of any high-tech pillow talk from the lips of someone like Jensen Huang would be very disturbing to the feds indeed. Both Nvidia and their "deeply sorry" CEO deny that he shared sensitive information beyond that required for routine customer/client discussions.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the company’s statement reads. "Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate."

In the US-Sino battle of artificial intelligence, Jensen Huang has – as with his marriage – played both sides. He’s undoubtedly been a, perhaps the driving force behind reinventing Nvidia from beloved makers of gaming gear to the US’ number-one purveyors of environment-ruining, brain-polluting slop technology. But after the Biden administration banned American-made GPU exports to China over fears they’d be used to boost the latter’s military capabilities, Huang successfully lobbied Donald Trump into relaxing those restrictions, allowing Nvidia to flog their wares – including their crème de la crème AI GPU, the H200 – to cash-rich Chinese companies.

In a further twist, many of those chips have got mysteriously stuck in Hong Kong import facilities, suggesting the Chinese government in fact wants AI companies to stick to Chinese-made parts. But then, the Hangzhou-based DeepSeek reportedly trained their latest AI model on illicitly-gained Nvidia tech, so there’s either a healthy black market in operation, or the CCP is willing to tolerate the occasional bit of decadent Western silicone if it helps them catch up to the burger-chomping likes of ChatGPT and Claude. Maybe both, and either way, one can see how a well-placed honeypot could prove useful. Allegedly.

Without wanting to pick sides, in a race where I hope both teams lose, it’s also China who have more work to do. The People’s Republic produces a greater proportion of successful 'open' AI models, where the inner workings and even source code is made public, and mines more of the crucial minerals needed to build components and infrastructure. However, US-produced 'closed' models dominate global AI usage, and despite the lack of minerals, its existing data centres are estimated to wield 40 times the combined compute power of China’s. Probably because they just get all the RAM they need from Best Buy instead of digging it up themselves.

The series is being led by Terry Matalas, the showrunner behind VisionQuest

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Netflix has announced that Planeswalker, an animated series based on Magic: The Gathering, will debut in 2027. The first sneak peek doesn't show much, but it does suggest that the show is taking several pages from the streamer's wildly popular League of Legends series, Arcane.

The series "chronicles the fierce clash between formidable mages known as Planeswalkers. At the center of this struggle for power and survival burns Chandra, a volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts and haunted by her past," according to the official synopsis.

"Confronted by an insidious force, Chandra and some of the most legendary Planeswalkers must harness their extraordinary abilities, navigate treacherous alliances, and battle their own inner demons to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence. As the line between victory and annihilation grows thinner, a single spark determines the fate of thousands of worlds."

The video above is filled with concept and previsualization clips, but there are a few seconds of what appears to be near-final animation and, well, it's tough to deny a clear Arcane influence here in the character design and animation style. The series is being created by animation studio Digic Pictures, which has previously made cutscenes for games including Assassin's Creed Shadows and Call of Duty: Vanguard, and led several episodes of Amazon's Secret Level series.

Terry Matalas, who served as showrunner for VisionQuest and seasons 2 and 3 of Star Trek: Picard, will be showrunner for Planeswalker. Cindy Appel, who wrote episodes for both those shows, serves as co-showrunner. Patrick Osborne is supervising director and executive producer.

Netflix has been trying to get a Magic: The Gathering series underway since at least 2019, when the streamer announced that the Russo brothers were attached to the project. Whatever vision they had for the series seemingly fell through, as it was five years before we heard about it again – this time, led by Matalas.

In the meantime, check out our guides to the best shows on Netflix and the best movies on Netflix to find out what you should be streaming today.

#3966. Wardogs Season 3 brings an urban map, Limited Mode, and a 185,000-account ban wave

Wardogs' Season 3 will launch on 12th November, complete with a new urban map, a new Limited Mode, and a ban wave targeting 185,000 accounts.

Developer Bulkhead confirmed the details earlier this week, revealing plans for a full wipe and progression changes that it hopes will "recapture the shared discovery and sense of achievement that defined" the 100-player tactical shooter when it first launched in Early Access.

The new map will focus on close-quarters fighting, and for a "more level playing field", players can dip into Limited Mode, which offers "an alternative way to experience" the game as it restricts weapons, ammunition, armour, and vehicles.

While the full list of restrictions is still being decided, it currently includes FMJ-only ammunition, a Tier 2 armour cap, and a reduced attack vehicle selection.

"The mode is designed to preserve the feel of early-to-mid-game combat and reduce the advantage offered by more powerful equipment," the team said.

Bulkhead also confirmed seasons are getting longer. From now on, they’ll last three months, giving players "more time to work towards their goals before each wipe and the development team more time to prepare future updates". Progression will also be "brought closer to the pace of Season 1", following the studio’s acknowledgement that Season 2 accelerated "the journey too aggressively".

"Season 3 is about giving players a new battlefield to learn together and a progression journey worth spending time on," said Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer. "Longer seasons give everyone more room to reach their own goals, and give us the time to properly develop what comes next."

Alongside Season 3, Bulkhead revealed it has used machine learning to review is "activating further layers of its anti-cheat" after analysing 187 million hours of gameplay with help from machine learning. It says having close to four million unique players since launch gave it enough data to pull that work forward from next year.

"[E]xploiters, real-money traders, and gold-farming networks" have been permanently banned and lost their server-hosting privileges, and a player trust score is planned for 2027.

"Protecting the people who play Wardogs fairly is essential to everything we're building," Brammer added.

Bigger changes to the metagame, including a new progression system, are also due in 2027 as Bulkhead works towards Wardogs 1.0. Full Season 3 patch notes will be out before launch.

Wardogs launched in Steam Early Access on 10th September, and is due on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S in 2028.

Wardogs is one of the breakout successes of the year. In our early access Wardogs review, we said the game's mix of competitive shooters' best bits with something entirely of its own made it "a brilliantly refreshing take on the genre".

#3964. Assassin's Creed is reportedly going to ancient Rome, while a mobile spin-off heads to Jerusalem

Ubisoft is reportedly working on two new Assassin's Creed games, and one of them is set in ancient Rome.

That's according to YouTuber Xj0nathan, who says the Rome game is codenamed Mars. He claims two sources with access to Ubisoft's backend systems backed up the information, and that the setting will likely be linked to the upcoming Assassin's Creed TV series.

The second game, codenamed Pocket, is said to be a mobile title set in Jerusalem. Xj0nathan claims it'll play a bit like Assassin’s Creed Valhalla’s Mastery Challenge, and look similar to the most recent Prince of Persia. The hero's mentor is apparently a character called Myriam.

Insider Gaming says it's heard the codenames too, but couldn't confirm them well enough to report them independently. It puts some of that down to the turbulence the franchise has gone through since former Assassin's Creed boss Marc-Alexis Côté left Ubisoft.

Last month, the outlet's sources also claimed Assassin's Creed Hexe, the next mainline game, had been delayed internally by another year, likely to 2028. Other reports claim we'll see it next year.

If Mars does move into full production, don't hold your breath - Insider Gaming doesn't expect us to hear anything about it until 2029 or 2030.

Assassin's Creed has visited Rome before, in 2010’s Brotherhood, but that was the Renaissance version of the city.

The leak comes less than a week after Ubisoft issued a statement about the future of the Assassin's Creed series, insisting there are currently no new remakes of the series' past games in the works.

Not only did it not get a price cut, it got several price increases

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Somehow, some way, the PS5 has been an extraordinary sales success despite launching in the middle of a global pandemic that caused massive supply chain issues and continuing on today amidst an unprecedented memory shortage and economic headwinds driving hardware prices sky high. Despite it all, people are buying PS5s, and many of them.

Sony confirmed just this week that PS5 has hit an incredible milestone of 100 million units sold in its six years on the market. That's not quite as fast as the PS2 or PS4, but it's a much more impressive achievement when you consider one crucial difference between the current-gen PlayStation and literally every other generation before it. Typically, games consoles decrease in price throughout their life cycles, but because of the disadvantages outlined above, the PS5 has only gotten more expensive, right alongside its competitors, the Xbox Series X/S and Nintendo Switch 2.

So, even though the PS5 failed to hit 100 million units sold faster than its predecessors, it still reached the record for units sold without any sort of permanent price cut from Sony. And before you head to the comments section to point out that you got a PS5 at a discount for Black Friday one year, we're talking about official, permanent price decreases from Sony, not temporary sales from retailers. That is seriously impressive considering the economic difficulties not only Sony and other hardware manufacturers are grappling with today, but consumers as well.

You could almost, almost make the case for PS5 being the first console period to hit that sales milestone without a price cut, but for the mighty Nintendo Switch. The Switch hit 100 million units sold in December 2021, and Nintendo never lowered its price globally. There was a price cut in Europe in September 2021, notably just before the Switch reached 100 million units, but it doesn't feel fair disqualifying it from claiming Sony's title for a small, regional price decrease alone.

Resident Evil Requiem's physical PS5 sales were nearly twice as large as its total Xbox sales, analyst finds

#3962. "The lesson learned is you can have both": Skyrim lead designer reckons there's merit in Baldur's Gate 3-style tough choices and Bethesda's do-anything approach

How many doors should be open at any point in an adventure?

Whether RPGs are better off prioritising player freedom or endeavouring to have several doors slam shut every time you put another foot forwards in order to encourage multiple runs with different characters is, to put it bluntly, something I reckon will still be a matter of debate in the year 4000. We'll all have evolved in non-corporeal beings floating in a galaxy that's been racked by such change that even the six million copies of The Elder Scrolls 5 we've littered the Earth with will have been swept away into the great recycling bin on the gods' desktop, and there'll still be sniping going on about whether it's ok that Skyrim lets you be a master thiefssassin who leads the companions, knows every spell under the sun, and slapped up a world-eating dragon for fun.

For what it's worth, the game's lead designer reckons both games that do and don't let you do that have their merits when executed well.

Speaking to The Examined Game, ex-Bethesda dev Bruce Nesmith talked about being "pleasantly surprised" when playing Baldur's Gate 3 just how much he enjoyed making "consequential decisions that closed off gameplay". In Nesmith's view, Larian "redefined things in a certain way" with their take on the D&D universe and the fantasy rules it plays by. However, he argued that there's still merit to taking an approach more akin to Bethesda's post-Morrowind Elder Scrolls entries and striving to make it possible for the player to see the majority of what the game has to offer in a single playthrough.

"They were both fun," he said. "They were just fun in different ways and that to me was part of the surprise. I would have expected to fall on one side or the other, as if they were things that you couldn't have both [of]. The lesson learned is you can have both. I can enjoy this game over here that does it this way and enjoy this game over here that does it that way."

Nesmith made clear that he still thinks the idea of, with a few exceptions like Skyrim's civil war, not gating the player off from the likes of doing multiple faction questlines is a "very good philosophy" that he supports.

As much as it's always a bit of a cop out to declare that everything's equally good, actually, I do think that there's merit in both approaches. I love the dedication the likes of New Vegas, Disco Elysium, and The Witcher 2 have to making you pick a path and see where it takes you at the expense of not seeing other stuff. Hell, the latter game's infamous for being totally different depending on who you choose to waltz off with at the end of the opening act.

That said, Skyrim's open-endedness was undoubtedly one of the factors which made it so easy for me to get majorly into when I was just cutting my teeth in RPGs as a teenager. There's value in such games existing, even if for plenty it might be as a gateway drug to games with crunchier and more challenging narratives that do demand you plug in your brain and carefully consider every choice you make. Whether there's still as much value in being the gateway drug nowadays compared to in 2011 is the question The Elder Scrolls 6'll likely answer whenever it rocks up. Coming as it is after the likes of BG3 and The Witcher 3 have had near Skyrim-level gangbusters success while leaning a lot more heavily into the hard stuff typically pegged as having less potential for mass appeal.

For what it's worth, while you can very much argue about the execution, Fallout 4's main quest was a lot more choice-heavy than Fallout 3's. So, Bethesda may well opt to pivot or make compromises in their player freedom-first ways if they feel some crunchier choice is in order.

#3961. Sony delays PlayStation's Pulse Elevate speakers indefinitely, less than a week before launch

Sony has delayed its Pulse Elevate wireless speakers indefinitely, less than a week before they were due to launch.

The news came in a 6th November update to Sony’s original announcement on the PlayStation Blog, first spotted by IGN. Quality testing has turned up a "production issue", Sony said, and there's no new release date yet.

"As part of our ongoing quality testing of Pulse Elevate speakers, we have identified a production issue with the product and have made the decision to delay the launch," the statement reads. "The additional time will allow us to ensure the product will deliver the experience we intended for our players. We apologise for the delay and appreciate your patience and understanding. We look forward to bringing Pulse Elevate to players soon."

The speakers were set to go on sale worldwide on 12th November, and pre-orders opened in September. It's unclear what, exactly, happens to those orders, but we'll update as and when we find out more.

Sony revealed Pulse Elevate in September 2025 as its first wireless speakers for desktop gaming. They sit alongside the Pulse Elite headset and Pulse Explore earbuds, and cost £199.99 ($219.99).

They connect to PS5, PC, Mac, and PlayStation Portal via PlayStation Link, and can pair with a phone over Bluetooth at the same time. There's also a microphone in the right speaker with what Sony calls "AI-enhanced noise rejection".

Midnight Black was due to be available everywhere, while the White version was limited to a handful of countries, including the UK.

Alongside the Pulse Elevate speakers, Sony revealed a range of hardware in September 2025, including a 27-inch gaming monitor that's coming only to the US and Japan.

#3960. Guide: GTA 6 Release Times: All The Key Details Xbox Players Need To Know

It's finally here! We've officially reached the launch week of GTA 6 on Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, PS5 and even the Xbox One (kind of), 13 long years since the most recent entry in the series back in 2013.

With that in mind, we thought we'd put up a quick release times guide so you know exactly when you can start playing the game, and we've also thrown in a few extra details about what we're expecting for Xbox One players at launch.

So, here are all the deets you need to know for Thursday!

On this page: GTA 6 Release Times: All The Key Details Xbox Players Need To Know

The official GTA 6 release date is Thursday, November 19th. You may still see people playing it on Wednesday though, as depending on where you live, certain players will be getting access to it earlier than others.

GTA 6 releases at midnight local time around the world. This means you'll be able to start playing it on Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S and PS5 as soon as November 18th turns into November 19th in your region.

Here's how it all works out based on a Universal Coordinated Time (UTC) time zone, for example:

Technically, yes. Due to the staggered rollout, players in New Zealand will be getting first access to GTA 6 at midnight in their time zone, which equates to 11am on November 18th here in the UK, and even earlier in the United States.

We urge caution around this, as Xbox's terms of service specifically state that you shouldn't switch regions unless you're actually located in the country you're switching to, but we'll leave the decision up to you.

News Here's What Xbox Owners Need To Know About 'Moving To New Zealand' For GTA 6

You may have noticed that we didn't mention Xbox One in the release times section up above, and that's because we don't quite know what's happening with it. In a nutshell, Xbox One players will be forced to use Xbox Cloud Gaming in order to get access to GTA 6, which in theory should require buying the game before access is granted.

There are too many unknowns ahead of launch about how this works though. Will cloud access be made available immediately? Will you be able to use the free-with-ads version of the cloud to play GTA 6, or will it require paying for the service? Is it just Xbox One that you can play it on, or will mobile and PC devices be supported too?

That's where we stand ahead of launch, so while GTA 6 definitely will be playable through the cloud on Xbox One in some form, it's probably best to wait until it's been released before handing over any money as things stand.

News GTA 6 Will Be Playable On Xbox One Through Xbox Cloud Gaming

Rockstar also confirms GTA 6 will run at 30FPS

Of course, we've already talked about the preload for GTA 6 and how anyone can download the game right now on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, regardless of whether they've actually bought it or not.

All that's left is to wait a few more days until the new Grand Theft Auto finally becomes available, and we can't wait to see whether it'll live up to the hype and become a Game of the Year contender when it arrives this Thursday.

#3959. Feature: 80+ PS5, PS4 Games to Buy in PS Store's Updated Black Friday Sale

PS5 and PS4 games going cheap we recommend

The PS Store's Black Friday sale is on now, running until 30th November, 2026 — and it's just been refreshed with even more discounts.

As with nearly every offer in Sony's digital store, there are literally thousands of PS5 and PS4 games going cheap. Obviously, nobody has the time to scroll through all those deals, which is where this guide hopefully comes in handy.

We've put together a (relatively) shorter list of some of the games we'd highly recommend while they're on offer.

Everything listed here comes with at least a 7/10 score from Push Square, and every game is at its lowest price point, with some setting new lows in this sale.

Discounted prices are shown in bold, and games at a new lowest-ever price are bold and underlined.

If you need to top up your PSN wallet, we've got you covered:

Please note that some external links on this page are affiliate links, which means if you click them and make a purchase we may receive a small percentage of the sale. Please read our FTC Disclosure for more information.

Let's have a look at some of the best games in the Black Friday sale.

The best James Bond game in a very long time, 007 First Light revives the character in brilliant style. Telling the origin story of the would-be spy, the game is a combination of sandbox-like, open-ended missions and linear set pieces and narrative moments, resulting in a highly appealing blockbuster. It tells a decent story, establishes fantastic new takes on well-known characters, and sets a solid foundation with great espionage and action gameplay.

1000xRESIST is all in on story, and this laser focus allows it to tell one of the most captivating and intriguing experiences you can have in video games. This sci-fi adventure sees an alien disease almost wipe out humanity, but one person is immune, and they rebuild society underground by cloning her. Combining visual novel elements with exploration, it's not the most challenging game to play, but its narrative more than makes it worthwhile.

If you're looking for a chilled out puzzle game to wind down with, A Monster's Expedition comes highly recommended. It's one of those puzzlers with a seemingly straightforward set of mechanics, but it uses them in increasingly smart ways to really test your brainpower. Set across hundreds of tiny islands you need to navigate by pushing logs into the water, its forgiving nature and gentle presentation make it a lovely game to get lost in.

A whimsical, miniature open world awaits in A Short Hike. From a top-down perspective, you explore an island with lots of interesting places to visit and adorable characters, each of whom has a task for you. This laid back experience is a true joy as you gain new abilities, collect things, and discover new areas.

Absolum is both a brilliantly crafted beat-'em-up and a devilishly addictive roguelike. Although the overall experience does feel slightly short-lived, you'll seriously struggle to tear yourself away from the game's striking fantasy world — especially when all of its systems start to click.

ARC Raiders is a phenomenal showcase of what immersive multiplayer can be. Every run is different, and your squad will come out with stories to tell each time. It can be tougher on those planning to play solo, and the extraction loop won't be for everyone. But as far as extraction shooters go, this is one of the most accessible, and it respects your time, giving you a fun experience from your first match. We can easily say that ARC Raiders is one of the best multiplayer games this generation.

Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure is a delightfully inventive puzzle game that weaves in a neat narrative to pull you through. Playing as a character that literally moves the world around her as she goes, this is effectively a series of slide puzzles set within a fleshed out world full of whimsical character. Always building on its core idea in imaginative ways, this is brilliant fun from start to finish.

Building upon the great foundations laid in Astro's Playroom, Astro Bot is the full-blown 3D platformer the little robot deserves. It's an explosion of creativity and fun; there is something new to discover in practically every level, and all of it is purpose built to put a smile on your face. Not only is it bursting with imagination, it's also executed brilliantly. The controls are spot on, every new mechanic and power-up is fun to use, and it's all presented with incredibly sharp visuals and flawless performance. The icing on the cake is its celebration of PlayStation's past 30 years, with delightful nods to hundreds of classics. We can't recommend this highly enough.

While many of the included games may border on unplayable from a modern perspective, the painstaking attention to detail in Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration is extremely easy to appreciate. The museum-like carousel of content, from interviews through to original artwork, is presented so handsomely that you can’t not get swept up in Atari’s dramatic story. And the fact that there over 100 of the company’s most famous titles, emulated excellently with their original instruction manuals available to pore over, adds playable context to a lot of the content. This is just an impressive overall experience that will appeal to those who lived through the rise (and fall) of Atari, as well as younger players eager to learn a little more about one of the industry’s true pioneers.

Avowed is arguably Obsidian's strongest modern release, and it's not for the reasons that you may think. While the game's writing and storytelling often lack bite and excitement, its gameplay saves the day with a cracking combat system, meaningful player choice, and the enjoyable exploration of some truly stunning locales.

Ball X Pit is a dangerously addictive roguelite that combines the speedy runs and rapid leveling up of Vampire Survivors with the ball-bouncing action of Breakout. It's one of those concepts that'll make you question why a game like it hasn't been done before, because it works brilliantly. Every element of the game feeds into something else, and the result is this incredibly compelling game that has a surprising amount to see and do.

Battle Chef Brigade Deluxe is the definitive version of this unusual but great culinary adventure. Set in a world where chefs go head-to-head in a prestigious cooking tournament, the game is half action title and half cooking minigames. You'll go out slaying monsters and harvesting ingredients, then brew them up to create delicious dishes to satisfy the judges. It's an odd recipe, but results in a surprisingly tasty dish.

Battlefield 6 is a phenomenal multiplayer experience that immerses and impresses with its chaotic mix of tight gunplay, best-in-class audio design, and the cinematic flair that made us love the series in the first place. The campaign isn’t anything to write home about, and Portal has yet to fully prove its worth, but they act as additions to what is easily the best Battlefield in over a decade.

A true cult classic, Beyond Good & Evil: 20th Anniversary Edition is a lovely remaster of a PS2 favourite. Playing as freedom fighter Jade, this unique sci-fi adventure has you exploring a weird and wonderful world through the lens of her camera. The remaster brings the visuals up to date and throws in some quality-of-life improvements, but the main reason to play this is for the great story and characters, which remain fresh and charming to this day.

Broken Sword: Shadow of the Templars is a sacred text in the history of point-and-click adventure games, and new remaster Reforged is the best version of the game that's ever been released. Quality-of-life improvements mean players who just want to enjoy the story without too much lateral thinking can do so, while veterans of the genre or returning fans can play the game in its original form, goats and all. Paris in the fall has never been more beautiful.

There have been climbing games before, but Cairn is a really unique example. To scale the huge Mount Kami, you need to control Aava's limbs individually, looking out for the best holds as you inch upward. On top of the challenging, physics-based mountaineering, you also need to keep on top of her health and hunger, but these survival aspects never feel too overbearing. It's a nicely balanced game with climbing that feels tangible and realistically tough.

Half interactive story, half cube-based puzzler, Catherine: Full Body is the expanded remaster of Atlus' brilliantly weird take on love. You play as Vincent, a 32-year-old bachelor who can't quite decide if he wants to commit to his long-term girlfriend. His potential infidelity gives way to suspiciously vivid nightmares where he's forced to scramble up towers made of blocks, lest he wake up dead. It's as mental as it sounds, but the tactile puzzles are addictive, and the storytelling is gripping at its best.

From the makers of TowerFall Ascension, Celeste is a pure platformer that provides a stern challenge. Using a straightforward set of moves, it does a lot with very little, but it's not just gameplay where it impresses. Madeline's climb up Celeste Mountain is both literal and metaphorical as she struggles to overcome her inner demons. Wonderfully pairing a touching story with rock solid platforming, this is one indie adventure that'll stay with you.

Creaks is one of PS4's very best puzzle games. Its commitment to continually evolving its mechanics makes for a phenomenal puzzling experience packed full of surprises and elating moments. With a stunning art style to boot as well as a narrative which reveals itself in all the right ways, Creaks offers an unforgettable ride that can be considered truly special.

Some say there are too many Metroidvania games for this world, yet when one as good as Crypt Custodian comes along, it serves as a reminder of exactly why so many developers chase that addictive fusion of explorative action. With shades of Death's Door and Tunic, brotherly duo Kyle and Eric Thompson have made an approachable yet exceedingly enjoyable adventure full of combat, platforming, puzzles, and charm.

Masterful in its storytelling, characters, and visuals, Kojima Productions went bigger and better with a sequel that comfortably dwarfs what the Japanese team achieved in its first delivery experience. Main character Sam is once again tasked with reconnecting a land mass to the chiral network, but this time his deliveries are further and expanded to encompass proper combat scenarios. Death Stranding 2 is a cinematic achievement on all fronts that will remain one of the crown jewels of the PS5 library forever.

Stephen has been part of the Push Square team for over six years, bringing boundless enthusiasm and a deep knowledge of video games to his role as Assistant Editor. Having grown up playing every PlayStation console to date, he's developed an eclectic taste, with particular passion for indie games, arcade racers, and puzzlers. He's also our go-to guy for Sonic-related matters, much to his delight/chagrin.

#3958. Star Wars Zero Company studio Bit Reactor lays off staff, a month after bringing furloughed developers back

"While it stings, I'm really proud of what we built together."

Star Wars Zero Company developer Bit Reactor has laid off an unspecified number of staff, a month after bringing some of its furloughed team back to work.

Several developers announced on LinkedIn on Friday, 6th November, that they had been let go, as first reported by Bespin Bulletin. Bit Reactor hasn't said how many people are affected.

Among them is senior environment artist Ryan Lopez, who spent three and a half years working on Zero Company, from pre-production to launch, and was laid off after a three-month furlough. UI engineer Tyler Eichten, who worked on much of the on-screen UI for the game's tactical missions, and Ryan Mosher from the QA team have also confirmed they were let go.

"While it stings, I'm really proud of what we built together," Lopez wrote. "It was a privilege to ship a game with you."

Bit Reactor furloughed most of its staff in the weeks before Zero Company launched on 27th August, with one source putting the figure at roughly 80 percent. The studio appeared to have run out of money just short of release.

The game did well regardless, and is thought to have sold more than a million copies within a month. Then, in a message shared on Bluesky on 7th October, CEO Greg Foertsch said the studio had "started the process of returning more of our team back to work". Asking staff to step away so close to launch was "an incredibly difficult decision", he said, "but one that was necessary to help us eventually bring as many people back as possible".

It's thought more than half the studio returned, though not everyone went back on full pay. It's not clear whether any of those who returned were among the people laid off this week.

In Eurogamer's Star Wars Zero Company review, we awarded the game four out of five stars, saying, "an already winning genre is matched with the perfect setting in this earnest, heartfelt, smart and slightly ramshackle turn-based tactics gem".

We've had two great Star Wars games this year, probably because Lucasfilm Games says it's now "more flexible" about who it takes pitches from

#3957. Microsoft workers accuse company of trying to get customers "addicted" to AI while forcing it on their own staff and making them party to "human rights violations"

Open letter warns of "a cascade of business and ethics risks"

A group of "concerned Microsoft workers" have published an open letter criticising their employer's "speed-at-all-costs" approach to generative AI, which they argue is "harming our customers, colleagues, shareholders, vendors, and the planet". They accuse Microsoft leadership of trying to get people "addicted" to genAI, while making their own staff miserable by mandating AI usage.

Echoing the on-going BDS campaign against Microsoft's Xbox business, the writers contend that Microsoft have become party to "human rights violations" by selling generative AI technology to Israel's military during the latter's invasion of Gaza, which a UN commission has deemed a genocide. They're also critical of Microsoft's contracts with the USA's draconian Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. While seemingly not against generative AI in principle, they're organising against "the AI industry’s trajectory to continue to enrich AI’s powerful few", pointing out that AI companies now account for a terrifying share of the global stock market.

I know about the letter thanks to Vertical Slice, who cite a New York Times report on Microsoft's recent voluntary buyouts, which follow several waves of mass layoffs at a company with a market value of around $4 trillion.

"For many, working at Microsoft has become joyless and demoralizing, with job satisfaction declining around the same time the company accelerated its AI investments," the workers write. "Crushing workloads, threats of AI job replacement and layoffs, constantly shifting business priorities, and re-orgs destabilize our work environment and erode employee trust in leadership."

The letter organisers complain that "workers are forced to use AI in almost every work area, with little to no training and no strategic rationale besides 'speed'," obliging them to spend a lot of time "learning and relearning tools, fixing AI slop, and reworking or rolling back low-quality features". They feel that Microsoft's generative AI strategy is exposing customers "to overreliance, misuse, and physical and mental harm", not least because "our own research shows that AI agents don’t prioritize user safety, and internal planning documents detail how to 'make people addicted' to AI products." If that last part is an actual quote from an internal feature document, then: yeeeeeeesh.

The writers further take issue with Microsoft's investments in data centers for generative AI use, which may use up a lot of water while contributing to carbon emissions (jeopardising Microsoft's older commitments to reducing their carbon footprint). They note that "our Community-First AI Infrastructure plan makes vague financial and job-creation commitments, but doesn’t address greenhouse gas emissions or other damage already being done."

The organisers also call out their employer for becoming "a partner to human rights violations" by licensing generative AI tools to the Israeli military and ICE. "Not only are we risking reputational, financial, and legal damage, we are allowing our AI products to be used against whole communities for mass surveillance, detainment, deportation, and genocide," they write.

Finally, they take a swing at "Microsoft’s participation in circular investment across a handful of AI leaders " - that is, AI companies pouring cash into each other, which naturally creates the risk of several companies biting the dust if one company's fortunes take a tumble. This ouroboros strategy "exposes workers, customers, shareholders, and society to a cascade of business and ethics risks," the writers claim, noting that AI-linked stocks now dominate the S&P 500 index.

The letter writers have a number of demands. They'd like more say over "AI product strategy decisions", and for Microsoft to consider customer feedback and bring different development disciplines together "to help guard against shipping AI-worsened user experiences". They want Microsoft to "offer quality training and empower workers to integrate AI in their workflows without tying AI use to rewards, reprimand or layoffs." They call on the execs to "end unfair AI-driven workforce reductions and agree to worker protections".

Looking beyond Microsoft's walls, the workers argue that "job opportunities from data center investments are mostly temporary" and that "Microsoft must protect all workers, not attempt to avoid the unionized trades in local communities, and ensure a just transition for all impacted workers."

The letter writers call on Microsoft to "expand Responsible AI and Sensitive Use teams and fund programs to communicate potential harms to users". They would like Microsoft to stop selling AI materials to organisations "if they are engaged in violence, mass surveillance, detainment, deportation, or genocide", requesting that Microsoft "transparently share contracts with all governments and their agencies or contractors, including police and armed forces, and immediately terminate any contracts with those directly or indirectly involved in human rights violations."

The letter writers want Microsoft to "reduce financial dependency on OpenAI and other AI partners and provide transparency into all AI investments". In general, they want their bosses to "stop offloading financial risk to workers, vendors, partners, customers, and shareholders through irresponsible investments and relationships." As regards the environment, the workers are demanding that Microsoft "reaffirm our goal to be carbon negative, water positive, and zero waste by 2030". They want Microsoft to cooperate more with environmental regulators, and "to respect local communities by rejecting dirty energy, engaging fairly and transparently, and refusing to build in resource-scarce areas."

It's not clear who, exactly, is behind the letter, or how many others at Microsoft have signed as of writing. I've requested comment from Microsoft, and will update this piece as and when I hear more.

#3956. Cyberattack on Sega third-party newsletter distributor reportedly sees over two million email addresses leaked, but Sega accounts unaffected

Japanese email distribution firm Arara were the target of the attack

Sega have revealed that over two million email addresses have leaked due to a cyberattack on Japanese email delivery provider Arara, whom the Like A Dragon and Sonic publishers use to distribute newsletters. Sega and Arara are currently busy investigating what happened in the breach, which doesn't appear to have affected the Sega accounts you can use receive in-game rewards and access a calendar which reminds you when it's Kazuma Kiryu's birthday. The companies have urged those who signed up for the affected newsletters to be wary of potential phishing attempts.

According to Automaton, who've translated Sega's official press release about the cyberattack, 2,196,044 email addresses in total were affected. 92,273 of that number were linked to the newsletter distribution.

The company have listed some specific newsletter releases as having been affected, including two exhibition announcements for this year's Tokyo Game Show, the announcement of arcade rhythm game Chunithm Mate's launch, six newsletters about online character lottery service Sega Lucky Kuji Online, the launch of a rhythm game update dubbed Ongeki Re:Fresh Act.2, and the launch of another arcade rhythm game update called Maimai DX MAGiCAL. Number one, that's a lot of rhythm games, and number two, Sega have advised those who opted in and received those newsletters to watch out for fishing emails from people posing as being tied to Sega or Arara.

Sega reportedly confirmed that - as far as the affected emails go - no names, dates of birth, genders, residential addresses, phone numbers, credit card information, and passwords are known to have been leaked. There had also been no reports of cases where the leaked information had been misused as of the time Sega made their announcement. The company have naturally put distributing any further email newsletters through Arara on hold until their investigation's done and plan to reach out to each affected person individually once the full details of the leak have been confirmed.

While data breaches and cyberattacks are nothing new, there have been a fair few recently, with both Street Fighter makers Capcom and Kingdom Come Deliverance 2 devs Warhorse suffering incidents of their own last month.

#3955. WoW: Forever is the biggest launch in World of Warcraft history, says Blizzard

World of Warcraft: Forever is the biggest launch in the MMO's history, pulling in more concurrent players than any previous WoW launch.

Blizzard shared the news on social media yesterday (7th November), saying the new edition, which launched on 4th November, broke records for both peak concurrent players and returning players.

"Congratulations everyone, you made history!" the official World of Warcraft account posted. "This is all because of you, the players. From all of us, thank you!"

The game hasn't just tempted back lapsed players. In a follow-up post, executive producer and World of Warcraft vice president Holly Longdale said it brought in the most new players for a WoW launch in 15 years.

"Welcome all! We're so happy you're here experiencing Azeroth for the first time alongside those of us playing it for the first time... again," she wrote.

Wooo! Another statistic is filling our hearts -- we are seeing the most NEW players for a WoW launch in 15 YEARS!Welcome all! We’re so happy you’re here experiencing Azeroth for the first time alongside those of us playing it for the first time...AGAIN 😁 #WoWForever https://t.co/QPp3MDoVyr

Blizzard finally officially confirmed World of Warcraft: Forever at September's BlizzCon after fans were obsessing over colours as dataminers pulled hues from Blizzard's website that were labelled under a curious "wow 2" tag, leading many to speculate that this referred to the rumoured World of Warcraft Camelot, or as it's better known, "Classic Plus", much like how Blizzard is now expanding Diablo 2.

Blizzard hasn't shared any actual player numbers yet.

#3954. DOOM: The Dark Ages Revelations Gets A Major Free 'Slaughter Mode' Update Today

The release of DOOM: The Dark Ages Revelations saw critics heaping praise on the expansion earlier in 2026, to the point where it's actually even in the Game of the Year (or at least Expansion of the Year) conversation as things stand.

News Xbox Has Another Potential GOTY Candidate On Its Hands, Even Though It's Just DLC

The reviews for Revelations have been absurdly good

The DLC is getting even better today as well, as a new November 16th updating is introducing "Slaughter Mode - an endless combat challenge in which you need to tear through waves of hordes and unlock rewards along the way.

DOOM developer id Software says no two runs in Slaughter Mode are identical due to the random encounters it throws at you, and there will also be special unlockable skins and weekly challenges thrown into the mix.

"Complete rounds to earn Skulls, which unlock rewards such as Slaughter Mode-only Slayer skins, weapon skins for all modes and profile icons. You can also unlock tracks from Andrew Hulshult’s IDKFA soundtrack to play in both Slaughter Mode and the Ripatorium! Take on weekly challenges for more opportunities to earn rewards and show off your slaying prowess."

All of this is available to you if you own the Revelations DLC for DOOM: The Dark Ages already, or if you have the Premium / Premium Upgrade versions of DOOM: The Dark Ages.

Don't forget that the base game is currently included with Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, Premium and PC Game Pass as well, so if you just want the DLC to play on Game Pass, you're looking at paying £17.99 / $19.99 for it.

We'll leave you with more details about the new Slaughter Mode for DOOM The Dark Ages: Revelations below.

Tear through relentless, escalating and unpredictable waves of demonic hordes, carving out your personal best scores and unlocking rewards using the Skulls collected from the carnage. With each checkpoint reached, players must ask themselves if they want to cash in their run or risk it all for more slaughter. No two runs through Slaughter Mode are identical as you fight escalating rounds of random encounters, bosses and arenas, turning up the heat as you proceed further into your run.

"Physical" copies of GTA 6 started shipping out to early buyers this week, including several members of GamesRadar+ staff. As players start to worry that their codes may be stolen with a bizarre flashlight trick, we had to see if we could steal our own – and honestly, I wouldn't be too worried about the possibility.

Rockstar's approach to its code-in-box release of GTA 6 is slightly different from most publishers. Rather than including the game code printed on a slip of paper in the case, the code is printed inside the back cover art itself. Social media is starting to be washed over with reports that if you shine a very bright flashlight just right into the edge of a GTA 6 case, you can make out the code without even breaking the seal on the game.

I tried the trick with my own US copy of the PS5 physical edition, and it did not work. There's a strip of camouflage patterning underneath the code that renders it unreadable from the opposite side no matter how bright a light you shine at it. My colleague Catherine tried the trick with her UK PS5 copy, and same deal – the code is unreadable through that camo pattern.

There is a catch here: not every code-in-box copy of GTA 6 has the camo strip. I've combed through unboxing videos of the game, and while I can't find any examples of US copies without the protective camouflage, some copies with a PEGI rating only have a plain black strip in the background. This, it seems, is the one that could be vulnerable to the apparent flashlight trick.

However, I haven't managed to track down anybody reporting that they've fallen victim to a stolen code. Most retailers keep their games behind locked glass cases, so a prospective code thief would probably have to buy the game, hope that it's a black background version, get an unusually powerful flashlight, shine it in, and then convince the retailer to take the game back for a refund in order for anyone to fall afoul of the potential scam.

Is that a level of trouble anyone's willing to go to in order to play GTA 6 for free? Well, yeah, I guess so. But it's also not an issue unique to GTA's code-in-box release – I've had a few occasions where I've purchased a new, "sealed" copy of a traditional physical game only to find that someone had carefully snuck the disc out of the package and returned it to the retailer where I eventually bought it.

And, well, if you're that worried, you can just buy the game digitally. Yeah, I know, I'm the exact kind of sicko who bought the physical version to have a box on my shelf and a poster on my wall, but it's not as if there's a real difference between getting the box and just doing a digital GTA 6 pre-order. Now, if there was actually a map in the box, that might be a different story.

#3952. PS Plus Subscriptions on Sale Now, But There's a Big Catch

Update [Mon 16th Nov 2026, 10:15am]: Sony has now discounted its three PS Plus subscription tiers until 30th November 2026, revealing the sort of savings on offer to new members. They are:

Original Story: Sony has revealed its PS Plus membership at all three tiers will be going on sale from tomorrow, 16th November, for two weeks.

However, if you've been paying attention to how Sony handles this promotion in the last few years, then you will already know what's coming: the discounted prices only apply to new sign-ups; current members won't have access to them.

"Players in participating countries who join PlayStation Plus during PlayStation’s Black Friday promotion can save big on select memberships," Sony clarifies in an updated PlayStation Blog post. As it states, you have to "join" PS Plus during the Black Friday offer period to qualify, which lasts from 16th November to 30th November.

The only promotion open to current PS Plus members is a subscription upgrade to PS Plus Premium. Anyone at the PS Plus Essential or PS Plus Extra tiers can upgrade to PS Plus Premium at a discounted rate.

This is a tactic Sony has utilised for years now — it has not let you extend a PS Plus membership at the same tier for a very long time. Instead, the promotion once again only applies to PS5, PS4 owners joining PS Plus.

In fact, this year, Sony hasn't even revealed what the discount will be yet. Normally, the accompanying graphic tells you the sort of offers coming (usually 33% off), but the image above has nothing on it. We'll have to wait until tomorrow to find out what the PS Plus deal for Black Friday 2026 is.

How do you feel about the offer? Share your thoughts in the comments below.

#3951. Swarmbreaker is an uncommonly mesmerising tower defence game in which enemies "cluster, collide and flow like a fluid"

It is said that King Canute once placed his throne on the shore and commanded the sea not to get his feet wet, thus proving to his flattering courtiers that only God Almighty holds sway over the elements. "But sire!" I would have told him, if I'd been one of the aforesaid lickspittles. "Why not lay down spike strips and park a couple of flamethrowers in the shallows?" I would have said this because I have just been playing Swarmbreaker, a tower defence game that aims to prove there is no fluid body so awe-inspiring that it cannot be machine-gunned into submission.

In Swarmbreaker - which launches on Steam tomorrow, and still has a demo as of writing – you have to defend your rocketship against waves of insect aggressors, who spawn at the map's far corners. Between waves, you spend earnings from kills on turrets, barricades, troops, and upgrades for all the foregoing. Sounds like bog-standard attrition management, perhaps, but what lifts Swarmbreaker is the "swarm" part. The rapacious scuttlers come in several distinct varieties, but they also "cluster, collide and flow like a fluid".

The results are hypnotic: coloured particles burst from each burrow and course through the map's contours, pushing movable terrain elements and eroding your structures like acid. You can practically hear the oil derricks fizz as they are engulfed and chewed to a lumpy puddle of iridescent digestive enzymes. Speaking of which, the more oil derricks you save during each wave, the more cash you'll have to spend before the next, but committing to their protection obviously risks leaving your ship exposed. Your fallback option is an inexhaustible mouse-click-fired artillery cannon, but this won't save you if the bulk of the swarm makes it all the way to your doorstep.

I'm still not convinced this isn't a run-of-the-mill tower defender, beneath it all, but it's worth giving the demo a shot just to enjoy the swirling tidal dynamics of homocidal buglife. What would King Canute have made of it all? I think he would have stuck his throne right by the biggest burrow, surrounded by gravity traps and howitzers. "Back in your hole, hungry liquids!" he'd have bellowed, firing dual AK47s simultaneously. "The only god I recognise is efficient chokepoint management! Death to sense-of-flow! Death to trickle-down politics!"

"SIRE," I'd have told him sternly. "You are getting your metaphors confused. And also that is a total waste of howitzers - those things are best placed on hills." Read more on Steam.

#3950. Missing teenager rescued after reaching out to another player in Among Us

"Our priority in this case was the safe return of the minor victim."

A teenager who went missing in Utah more than 17 months ago has been rescued from a home in Oregon after she got in touch with another young player in Among Us.

According to a federal criminal complaint reported by Newsweek and KUTV (via IGN), the girl, who was 15 when she disappeared from Garden City, Utah, on 29th May 2025, began chatting with another teenager in Among Us on or around 15th October this year.

The pair later moved their conversation to a different social media app, where she told them who she was and that she was being held against her will in Oregon. She had been given a phone with no cellular data, which meant she could only get online via wi-fi.

The other teen told their parent, who contacted the FBI on 1st November. Agents listened in on a video call between the parent and the girl, and she was recovered from the house later that day. She is now 17.

Adam Hunter Harmel, 39, of Huntington, Oregon, was arrested during a traffic stop.

According to the US Attorney's Office for the District of Utah, he allegedly met the girl online in May 2025, then drove to Utah to pick her up and took her back to his home across state lines. He was charged on 2nd November with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity, and made his first court appearance in Boise, Idaho, on 4th November.

"Our priority in this case was the safe return of the minor victim," said US Attorney Melissa Holyoak. "Those who allegedly exploit and prey upon the most vulnerable members of our communities will be relentlessly investigated and held accountable."

Utah's US Attorney's Office stresses that a complaint is merely an allegation, and that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

#3949. Something Weird Is Going On With GoldenEye 007 And Xbox Game Pass

Earlier this month, you may recall that Xbox announced 14 games that would be leaving Game Pass in early November, with arguably the highlight of the bunch being the classic Rare FPS, GoldenEye 007.

We initially thought this might have been a mistake, but then Xbox doubled-down by announcing the game's departure in an official Xbox Wire roundup, confirming that it would definitely be leaving console and cloud on November 15th.

We're now on November 16th, and GoldenEye 007 remains included with Game Pass. Every other title from the list has been removed from the service, but Bond has defied the odds once again to remain part of the subscription!

So, what's going on here? It might take a while until we find out for sure, but we're going to guess that Xbox has either managed to arrange a deal to keep GoldenEye 007 on Game Pass, or they've just pushed back the removal date.

In any case, it's weird that nobody's said anything about this yet, and we're hoping we'll get clarification in the near future. GoldenEye has always been a game that's been tied up in licensing issues (hence why we never got the cancelled Xbox 360 version of it), but perhaps they've managed to figure out a long-term solution.

Anyway, we'll keep an eye on it, and this article will be updated with any important information that's revealed over the next few days. For now though, feel free to keep enjoying GoldenEye 007 on Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and Premium!

As the refounding theory finally starts to settle in, now we've got a shifting Great Calamity to deal with

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Legend of Zelda timeline has gotten yet another confusing new update, shifting the events leading to Breath of the Wild by 9,900 years and directly contradicting established lore. It's such an about-face for the existing story that series fans are pretty sure it's just a mistake, but the new word comes straight from Nintendo of America, which is often treated as gospel.

The Zelda timeline splits into three different branches based on the end of Ocarina of Time, but those branches all converge in the misty history leading up to the events of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. Earlier this year, Nintendo updated the Japanese version of the timeline and made clear that the founding of Hyrule depicted in flashback during Tears of the Kingdom shows the start of a new Hyrule, well after the one depicted in Ocarina of Time and other games has faded into history.

Now, Nintendo of America has updated the official English-language timeline to confirm the refounding – well, I say "confirm" but I'm sure it'll remain contentiously debated among the most dedicated purists. Either way, the update has made another curious tweak to the rest of the backstory.

Up until now, we've understood the timeline depicted in Tears of the Kingdom's flashbacks like this: Hyrule is (re)founded, Ganondorf appears to invade, and is sealed away as part of the Imprisoning War. Untold generations pass, and the evil entity known as Calamity Ganon eventually emerges and ravages the kingdom before being pushed back by Sheikah technology. 10,000 years pass from that Great Calamity, and that brings us to Breath of the Wild. Calamity Ganon reemerges, Link hibernates for 100 years, and the game begins.

According to the new timeline, the Imprisoning War happens, 9,900 years pass, and then the Great Calamity happens. Then it's just 100 years before Ganon reemerges – now referred to as "the second Great Calamity" – kicking off Link's century-long hibernation leading into Breath of the Wild.

In other words, the first Great Calamity, which was originally placed 10,000 years before Breath of the Wild, now takes place just a century or two before the game's events. This is despite the fact that Breath of the Wild is full of people trying to unlock the secrets of a pre-Calamity world that's long since faded into myth.

How are Zelda fans taking the sudden break in established lore? Well, you can read the Reddit threads for yourself, but I imagine you can already guess the tone of the responses. The Zelda timeline is notoriously convoluted, and while Nintendo has kept it up since at least 2003, Shigeru Miyamoto always maintained that it's "not that important to us."

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

Perhaps that's why Eiji Aonuma shut down attempts to add further nods to the timeline Ocarina of Time, and why a new official timeline update can so suddenly make an astronomical shift to established lore. Don't worry – regardless of how this detail shakes out, I'm sure the timeline will be broken in all-new ways soon enough.

Nintendo pulled back the horror from one of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake's most terrifying enemies: "Maybe we've gone a step too far."

#3947. Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy releases in January, leaving not very long to prepare for all the crunchy cRPG choices and secret wars it'll lob your way

Embrace the role of an Inquisitor in the grim darkness of the not so far away future

Oh shit, that's not too far away. Terrifyingly, that last sentence is now a thing I can accurately write about games coming out in January 2027. Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy has just been confirmed as one such game, with the cRPG's heresy investigation set to commence towards the end of the month.

January 28th, 2027, is the full Dark Heresy release date, as announced by devs Owlcat on Steam. The beta version of the game'll be closing down on January 7th to make way for the full game, so as of writing there's still some time to give that a go if you fancy.

If this is the first you've heard of Dark Heresy, here's Owlcat's synopsis of what it's all about:

Embrace the role of an Inquisitor in the grim darkness of the far future in a cRPG set in the rich Warhammer 40,000 universe. Start your service as an acolyte of the Inquisition: Investigate heresy, command a diverse warband, and shape the fate of the Calixis Sector in a story-rich experience where every decision has weight, justice is non-existent, and the line between salvation and damnation is razor-thin. Explore an in-depth depiction of the Inquisition as an organisation and the vast force it commands: its power, bureaucracy, and inner conflicts laid bare like never before.

As an Inquisitor, you have one primary goal: to protect the Imperium, whether that be from the taint of xenos, the betrayal of heretics, or the scourge of mutants, by any means necessary. Be the conduit of the Emperor’s will in a place where all hope was lost decades ago, explore the mysteries of the maddening Tyrant Star, and overcome the worst horrors thrown at you by the Noctis Aeterna.

A place where all hope was lost decades ago? You sure this is the Warhammerverse and not real life lads? I jest, but bursting into rooms and shouting 'Nobody expects the God-Emperor’s inquisition!' Monty Python-style does sound quite fun. Oisin's previously written in more depth about what Dark Heresy devs have said regarding what to expect from its investigations, if you want nitty-gritty details rather than references to sketch comedy.

If you're so inclined, Dark Heresy is wishlistable on Steam.

#3946. Don't be fooled by Horses of Hoofprint Bay's hand-drawn art, this stable management game has all the drama of a Jilly Cooper novel

Poema is my pride and joy. She was my first horse and she's a competition winner, but she's reached her potential. She'll never be a show jumper, and that's where the money and prestige are to be found. If I'm ever to grow my horse farm into a nationally renowned equestrian centre, I need the cash to expand and upgrade my facilities. Poema is a hoofstep on the path to that future, but she's not going to be able to take me all the way herself.

For all its hand-drawn aesthetics, Horses of Hoofprint Bay has hard realities like the limits of Poema's future bubbling under its surface. While the game's scripted narrative may be lacking, it's shockingly easy to fill in the gaps with drama worthy of a Jilly Cooper novel.

There may be better author comparisons, but I learned everything I know about showjumping from Cooper's Riders – much as I learned everything about independent television franchise bids in the '80s from its sequel Rivals – a book which is as much about the nitty gritty of horsetraining and competing as it is about toffs jumping into bed with one another. In my mind the two are tightly connected - showjumping and Jilly Cooper, not horses and toff bonking. In Horses of Hoofprint Bay, the only real story you get is the fact you've scrimped and saved to buy your first horse and your uncle has lent you the use of his field while you start your business. I was hoping there would at least be a similar setup to Regency Solitaire, where your motivation for touring the country's tearooms is motivated by paying off your brother's gambling debts. Yet, despite this disappointing start, I soon found its business simulation mechanics provide great storytelling material.

Horses of Hoofprint Bay has many of the trappings of a cosy game. At the start of each day, you'll prepare the stables, dragging a rake around the yard to sling away the manure, clicking buckets of water to refill the trough, and making sure there's enough hay for all the horses. But this isn't just for the larks, if you skip these tasks there are serious knock on effects for yours horses. Forget to brush down your horses' coats or pick out the stones in their shoes, and they're liable to develop saddle sores and other injuries when you ride them. Leave an abrasion untreated and it can develop into an infection. Even something like taking a dirty horse to a contest can cost you. I forgot to brush Poema before entering her into her first contest and despite taking first place, her embarrassingly unkempt coat lost my stable prestige. It was a cruel end to what should have been a great celebration.

So long as your horses are well rested, you can train them each day. You may want to take them through some confidence building lunges, where they need to walk, trot, and canter on demand, or a more physically demanding Cavaletti or showjumping course. These latter too are much more tiring, but they build a horse's strength and endurance. The higher its endurance the more energy it can expend on training sessions each day, and the higher its strength the more jumps it can do in succession before slowing to a walk for a breather - essential when you're competing in a timed competition. Overdo the exercise, however, and you'll exhaust a horse, severely reducing its energy for the next day.

Now, unlike Poema, my freshly bought stallion Kolizey has the potential to compete in showjumping competitions. He'll never go all the way to the big national contests, but he can take a ribbon in the district and regional contests. Or he will when he's up to standard; he's arrived from the breeder in a sorry state: brambles in his mane, mud on his flanks, stones in his shoes, and his strength and endurance are far too low to make it through an entire course of obstacles.

The biggest problem, however, is Kolizey's confidence: it's shot. I don't know what was happening in the stalls at the breeder's, but he arrived at my stables backing up at the first sign of a jump. Before I can hope to earn him his first ribbon, I have to build up our relationship. If we exercise together enough in the yard, his confidence will grow and he will follow my direction without question.

It may be getting ahead of myself, but I also have plans for Kolizey and Poema to produce a foal. Done right, the two should raise a horse that's able to exceed its parents' potential, becoming stronger and more endurant than both of them. A stronger horse means a ticket to the bigger contests and the bigger prize pots. Not that I can start breeding the two just yet. I want both horses to be at peak physical fitness. Poema's already there, while Kolizey can't even manage a jump without shying away.

While getting Koliszey contest ready, I still need to be bringing in cash. That means using Poema as a training horse for students' riding lessons. The better I am at the minigame where I use the Q, E, W, A, S, and D keys to tell them to sit forward or back, hold the reins higher or lower, or to level out their legs, the more they tip me. I have to be careful, because when Poema is working with students, she's not being stretched, and her strength and endurance can wither which means she struggles to maintain her winning streak in the contests.

Another reason to hold off on getting Poema pregnant is that during the second half of her pregnancy, she can't be ridden, which means no contests and no lessons for students. Currently, those are my two main sources of income besides what I'm paid in rent to board a couple of nearby farmers' horses. I don't want her out of the rota when Kolizey isn't yet ready to step into her place.

And, well, while I'm on the subject of plans, reader, I must tell you, the future lies in semen. If I can build the facilities, earn the cash, and raise Kolizey's profile, I can make a good buck on his virile stallion cream. With the money I bring in from a prizewinning semen I can expand into the far field, creating space to take on more horses, upgrade my home from the caravan I'm living in currently, maybe even build a proper training school. I'm not going to afford all that by giving riding lessons to the local children or boarders' rent. No, the big money comes from competition wins and valuable horse sauce.

While Poema continues entering contests and carrying students, I start pushing Kolizey harder. Multiple training sessions every day. I begin with Cavaletti, which is a kind of obedience competition. Your horse has to be travelling at the correct speed when it passes marker flags – walking, trotting, or cantering – and make some small jumps over cross bars. It should be straightforward, but because Kolizey's confidence is so low, he keeps refusing my orders and trying to change speed. He warns me before he's about to speed up or slow down, and if I counter it in time he will obey me and even receive a little confidence boost, but often he does it just before a jump, messing up my timing and he hits the bars. Each time he fails a jump it knocks his confidence, risking me taking me even further from where I need him to be.

I try the easier lunges sessions. And they raise his confidence a little but they're doing little for his physical health. It's all taking too long and Poema's getting older every day. In a fit of frustration, and in mark that I may not be able to cut it as an animal trainer, I skip from the Cavaletti training straight into a showjumping qualifier. The time limits on these are much stricter, so you have to clear the course at a gallop. This is also where a horse's strength really comes into play. The faster you're going, the more strength it requires to jump an obstacle. Horses only recover strength when moving at a walk, so you don't want to tire a horse out by going at a gallop through the whole course, else they won't have the strength to make all the jumps and they'll be forced to withdraw from the event. But nor do you want to go too slowly and fall foul of the time limit.

I realise my mistake as soon as the course begins: I try to stir Kolizey into a walk he refuses. Thankfully the timer only starts when he crosses the line, but it's an inauspicious start. I tap forward again and he begins to walk. I tap again and Kolizey moves up to a trot, then to a canter, before picking up to a gallop. I think he's going too fast as we approach the first jump, but Kolizey clears it. Then another jump and another. With a nervous eye on the depleting strength bar, I tap him down to a canter for the next jump. We're halfway through the course, I briefly slow to a walk to recover some strength then take the next three jumps at a canter. We're so close to the end now but a big yellow exclamation mark appears next to the strength bar. Kolizey is on the edge of exhaustion but he refuses to slow down and increases to a gallop for the last two jumps.

He completes the course with a perfect clear. Not a single obstacle clipped and we end with ten seconds left on the timer. Not only has Kolizey earned his showjumping license, his success swells his confidence. He's a natural athlete.

The next day, with my horses rested, I take Kolizey and Poema to town to compete in the showjumping and Caprilli events respectively. They both bring home first place, raising the prestige of my stables, earning me a tidy little packet, and convincing me it's time my prized horses started a family. I'm perhaps too eager, when I try to send them to the breeding station, I'm told they're both 'Done for the day'. I suppose I should give my contest winners a bit of a break. They've earned it. I groom them and send them both to bed with an apple as a treat.

Except, maybe they weren't too tired: the next morning, I'm met with a message telling me Poema is pregnant. My stable's become the Olympic Village, with my rosette-winning horses working out the highs and stresses of competition in the only way they know how. Good on them. I needn't have even made the breeding station.

Then, with horror, I remember the horses I'm boarding for the neighbours. They're both stallions themselves. Neither of them are at competition level, their strength and endurance is lower even than Poema's when she arrived at the stable. If either of them are the father, Poema is about to be out of action for a whole season and at the other end of it I'll have a foal that can't even compete in the beginner events. fetch the equestrian version of Hercule Poirot, I need to find out who impregnated my horse!

It may not be a plot worthy of Cooper, but it will do for me.

#3945. Saving Mass Effect would take $200m+, says BioWare co-founder

Anyone hoping to buy Mass Effect from EA and finish what BioWare started needs to get saving now, as it could cost over $200 million (£150m).

That's according to BioWare co-founder Trent Oster, who reckons that's what a new Mass Effect game would need to meet fans' expectations.

"The scary component of Mass Effect is the audience is going to want the best of 'AAA' development," Oster said on Twitter/X, as spotted by GamesRadar.

The scary component of Mass Effect is the audience is going to want the best of “AAA” development. Rough ballpark (based on contemporaries) is $200M+. That is a big number to commit up front. There has to be a bigger plan in place for the IP to make the math work.

"Rough ballpark (based on contemporaries) is $200M+. That is a big number to commit up front. There has to be a bigger plan in place for the IP to make the math work."

He did add that it could be done for less, though. "That said, I think it can be done well for less than that amount with a disciplined approach and an experienced team," Oster said.

"I think a game could be done cheaper, if you kept it simple and hit the big beats," he added in a separate tweet. "It wouldn’t be what the team described in the Universe concept. The big push would be getting the IP free. The fans deserve more than one game."

I think a game could be done cheaper, if you kept it simple and hit the big beats. It wouldn’t be what the team described in the Universe concept. The big push would be getting the IP free. The fans deserve more than one game.

Oster's comments come as the #SaveMassEffect campaign continues to grow following EA's decision to close BioWare and cancel Mass Effect 5. Fans want EA to keep making Mass Effect games, or hand the series over to a studio that will.

Oster has backed the campaign too. "I love seeing all the energy around #SaveMassEffect," he wrote on 4th November. "I think there is a still a great thesis for a well-funded RPG developer who can deliver. Makes me want to get some of the original band back together."

EA has not confirmed whether or not it would consider selling the IP.

The petition created to save BioWare's well-loved sci-fi RPG, Mass Effect, topped 185,000 signatures in just days. It's now exceeded 317,000. Joe Smith, credited with starting the petition, isn't necessarily asking EA to change its mind about BioWare; instead, the petition calls for "decisive action by committing to the continued development of Mass Effect".

We said a sad farewell to BioWare last month. The closure, which came just months after Saudi Arabia's $55bn leveraged buyout of EA, was anticipated by experts, but drew widespread condemnation and messages of sympathy from across the industry.

A new report claims EA closed BioWare because it was forced to choose between investing in one of two sci-fi projects: a new Mass Effect game or a new Star Wars Battlefront game. And it chose the latter.

Fans are trying other routes to keep BioWare's doors open, too. Canadian fans of the studio have escalated their grievances to the governmental level, calling on the Canadian Government to step in and save the studio from closure, seemingly after Canada's New Democratic Party leader Avi Lewis called on the government to do so.
