#3914. Nintendo's legendary Kirby designer Masahiro Sakurai weighs in on gen-AI, saying "it has yet to gain my trust" but not to reject it completely

"Doing nothing is probably not the right approach."

Masahiro Sakurai, the designer behind many iconic Nintendo franchises such as Super Smash Bros. and several Kirby titles, has weighed in on the ongoing discussion of generative-AI use in game development.

At an event celebrating the release of his new book - Masahiro Sakurai’s Thoughts on Games - the veteran director told Famitsu he hasn't and currently isn't using the technology to make games, noting that the role of a designer is to generate ideas.

"It has yet to gain my trust," Sakurai said via DeepL machine translation. Regarding graphical use specifically, he added that, "It must not amount to exploitation of any kind," and that "for the time being, we can produce better results by coming up with ideas ourselves".

But Sakurai is wary of rejecting gen-AI completely, saying "making games today is far too difficult", with some games "running at a loss even after selling millions of copies". A company in that position may go under if it does not change its stance on generative-AI, he suggested. "Doing nothing is probably not the right approach," he said, but "where and how to use it" is a complex topic with a lot of uncertainties. Sakurai is taking "a slow-paced approach" for now.

Outside of regular industry layoffs, the use of generative-AI in games has been the most controversial topic amongst developers and players. Some argue it's already being used in multiple development disciplines, notably programming and writing code. Others, such as Shigeru Miyamoto, are more sceptical of the technology's capabilities, especially when it comes to the more creative and art-driven parts of game development.

Certain things are synonymous with Grand Theft Auto - crime, cars, corruption, guns, mayhem and murder. You normally might not expect empathy from a game like GTA 6 with the series' past in mind, then, but Rockstar Games have added "mechanisms" to create empathy anyway.

GTA has always been somewhat of a cynical and comically rude franchise, but it seems Rockstar's now borrowing some lessons from its more grown-up Red Dead Redemption 2. Unrestrained violence and city-wide chaos will still be possible in Leonida - this is a GTA game, after all - but that's not all there is anymore.

Speaking to The Guardian (good spot, IGN), co-studio head Rob Nelson said "crime is a fundamental part of GTA - at least up until now, it has been." Rockstar is "trying to make sure we're not punishing people for playing the game they are used to," so you can still expect the freedom to get into car jams and push passerbys unprovoked (or worse). "[But] your actions will have some effect on how the game plays out."

When asked if GTA 6 is encouraging empathy in any way, Nelson agrees: "I would say that it's a product of the story we're trying to tell. We've tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to."

GTA 6 notably is the story of two people, Lucia and Jason. In a series full of protagonists who often care very little about anyone outside of their own interests, Lucia and Jason are almost the solar opposite - and quite fittingly, the upcoming game seems to nudge you into behaving differently because of this relationship.

#3911. Ahead of GTA 6 and as concerns over genAI PC ports grow, Take-Two's CEO says they're revving up their "technical defences" and "legal activites" over piracy

"[Piracy is] going to become more of a challenge… and we're aware of that"

It's a bit of a time for AI and games at the moment, 'ey? A bad time, obviously, as it's infecting everything from game development, to the modding community, to native PC ports of a remake of a very popular game that I won't link to for fear of a certain company finding out where I live and ending me there and then. And of course, the latter may be a concern for one Rockstar Games and the impending release of GTA 6. But according to Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, game's publisher, they are currently technically and legally preparing themselves.

IGN recently spoke to Zelnick regarding potential AI cloning concerns, notably about any business issues they may face as a result. "I don't think it’s a financial matter, in terms of a threat to our business," Zelnick explained. "I do think it’s a creative matter. It's important to everyone, our developers and our consumers alike, to deliver the experience Rockstar envisions. And at the same time, of course, we protect our intellectual property vigilantly. So we are focused on these concerns. We're not in the least cavalier about them. Technology is advancing quickly. And at the same time, I do think that pretty much everyone wants the Rockstar experience as Rockstar intended."

Zelnick also made a comment about thinking "all companies should be protecting intellectual property, their own and everyone else's," in response to a question about whether he wants to see OpenAI follow in Claude's footsteps by limiting the potential for genAI clones. "If you're in the intellectual property business, which Anthropic is and OpenAI is, then it seems ironic on the one hand to stomp on someone else's IP and hope that yours is protected," he said.

It was during an investor Q&A where Zelnick dug into the precautions Take-Two are take-twoing in regards to the growing threat of AI. "[Piracy is] going to become more of a challenge… and we're aware of that. So we are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defenses and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And at the same time, without in any way being cavalier, every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy. So this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it."

Essentially: unless you want to face the wrath of the kinds of lawyers multi-billion dollar companies can afford, I wouldn't bother trying to clone GTA 6 with AI! Probably won't end well!

#3910. Activision cracking down on popular Call of Duty: Warzone app that basically constituted cheating

"Lobby shopping" is what Call of Duty: Warzone players have been calling the ability to check the skill level of players in a lobby prior to joining it, enabling them to pass on those that include a lot of tough competition.

There are several ways players, notably Twitch streamers and content creators, have been able to do that over the years. But the use of one app in particular - Warzone Agent - has been considered by many to be cheating, and Activision is finally doing something about it.

Alongside the launch of Modern Warfare 4's version of Warzone and the game's first season of post-launch content, Call of Duty's anti-cheat team Ricochet has announced it's officially cracking down on Warzone Agent.

"Yesterday, we began taking action against Warzone Agent, a paid, unauthorised third party tool that lets users lobby shop in Warzone," the developer revealed in a post on X. "Ricochet anti-cheat will block players attempting to load the software and instruct them to unload it before accessing multiplayer."

Having the ability to cherrypick the lobby with the lowest-skilled players possible bypasses the game's matchmaking algorithm, potentially ruining the game for the dozens of other players in the match. Historically, content creators have used the app (and other methods) to post impressive kill records.

The developer added in a follow-up message that: "Using unauthorised software to manipulate the player experience violates Activision terms of use and leaves your account and hardware subject to enforcement." The language seems to stop just short of outright confirming those players using Warzone Agent will be banned.

As part of this crackdown, Ricochet reiterated its stance on boosting - artificially increasing (or decreasing) one's skill rating - saying that it too is considered cheating. "Receiving a boost, having another player log in to boost your account, or purchasing a boosted account are all against policy," the developer said.

"Boosting services flood lobbies with low effort accounts used to farm XP and complete challenges. Those accounts can later be sold as Ranked Play ready, directly feeding the cheating marketplace."

More than 20,000 boosting-related accounts have been removed since the launch of Modern Warfare 4, according to the developer, and Ricochet will "continue to apply pressure" in this area.

The quality of multiplayer was a particular highlight in Eurogamer's review of Modern Warfare 4, in which Dom Peppiatt lauded the complexity of weapon handling, which works without taking away from accessibility of the gunplay.

Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company after he admitted to an affair on Sunday, and allegations of a second affair came out on Wednesday. Now there are reports of a potential third. Though CTO Colette Kress has taken over in the interim, Nvidia seems to be shopping around for its next CEO, much to the dismay of some Nvidia staff, according to a report from Wired.

It's claimed that a longtime engineer at Nvidia took to an internal suggestion box this week to ask the Nvidia board to consider the company's employees before deciding whether or not to get rid of Huang. This note was made prior to his resignation.

However, over 1,600 comments have been left regarding this suggestion, the majority of which are apparently supportive of Huang. One says, "If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss."

Another claims, "We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance."

Notably, not all employees took to the suggestion box to air the same sentiment. One sent an email to the entire company saying, “I stand by Jensen. Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”

That email continues, “If America fails the man who helped build its future, then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

Jensen Huang's role in Nvidia can't be overstated. As the co-founder of the company, and President and CEO since 1993, he has no doubt been instrumental in its success. And business has been booming for the graphics card company-turned-AI company over the last few years.

We should hear more about Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic sometime next year, according to KOTOR and Mass Effect project director Casey Hudson.

The upcoming roleplaying game was announced about a year ago, but we haven't heard much from the exciting project since finding out that BioWare veteran Casey Hudson is at the helm... until now, that is.

Speaking to The Fourth Curtain podcast, which you can find below, Hudson teases his new game studio Arcanaut has "some pretty exciting things coming next year" in regards to the Star Wars RPG. "So we're going to be gradually rolling out some new announcements and information about the game, but, you know, you won't have to wait too long into next year before we'll have some things to share."

2027 marks Star Wars' 50th anniversary, with Disney promising a year-long celebration of its iconic sci-fi universe. Fate of the Old Republic could well show up as part of the company's festivities.

Despite the encouraging update, Hudson confirms there's no release date set in stone at the moment, though Arcanaut Studio is supposedly making steady progress on what he describes as a Knights of the Old Republic spiritual successor.

"I mean if you talk to folks at the studio, we work at a very brisk pace," Hudson says. "It's, on the one hand, challenging because we set a high bar for how quickly we can move, but, then, you look at where we get to - we work in six month cycles of big milestones every six months - and every six months we look at it and go, 'Oh my god, we've gone so far.' And so we're moving quickly through things. This isn't a project where we kind of wait around until the end to sort of figure out what we're doing."

#3907. Rockstar's doing a GTA 6 launch 'festival' in Miami featuring a lot of presumably expensive musical stars

The next-level glamour of Grand Theft Auto 6's arrival continues with word that Rockstar is hosting a star-studded launch 'festival' for the game in Miami - the game's setting-by-a-different-name.

The event will feature two stages hosting live performances by musical artists both featured in the game and from those who are not. Cardi B is probably the headliner - my knowledge of popular music is creaking here - but there's also Travis Scott, Don Toliver, Kodak Black, Sofaygo, Ca7riel, and Paco Amoroso.

Meanwhile, GTA 6 soundtrack duo Justice are doing a DJ set, as are The Dare with Fcukers, which is a dangerous name to spell. Also appearing: Metro Boomin, Nick León with DJ Python, Propsa with Skream, Rauw and Friends, Suero, and Tainy.

The event is being hosted at event space Mana Wynwood, and the pre-sale lottery for tickets begins this week on Wednesday, 11th November. Tickets are limited to two a head.

The full soundtrack for GTA 6 is yet to be revealed, with only a handful of songs so far detailed - featuring Rauw, Ca7riel, Paco Amoroso, and Travis Scott, among others. But of course music and radio stations play a huge role in the series, and given the amount of time we'll be playing GTA 6 and listening to these songs, it may well provide a lucrative platform to be featured on.

Meanwhile, the cultural impact of GTA 6's imminent arrival continues with a takeover of swanky department store Selfridges in London, which has a custom Ferrari parked in a window and an extensive range of expensive merch to buy.

It's not all good news for Rockstar, though. The company is also fighting an employment tribunal in Scotland relating to the sudden firing of 31 staff from Rockstar North this time last year. Rockstar alleges this was done for gross misconduct reasons, whereas the fired staff maintain it was done in the name of union busting. The results of that hearing are expected close to GTA 6's release, on 19th November.

#3906. Sony have cancelled Fairgame$, once again reminding us that chasing live service big bucks basically never works

You know, I'm sure that Sony had every intention of following through on their intention to release 10 live service games by 2026, as they mentioned way back in 2022. Well, as far as an intention that's designed to please shareholders can go, anyway. And now here we are, almost five years on from that comment that continues to haunt them with the news Fairgame$ has been cancelled.

This comes from a report from Bloomberg, who shared that, thankfully, there are no planned job cuts due to the game being cancelled. In a statement, Sony said that, "The studio will shift its focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation Studios, while also exploring new creative opportunities, though didn't go into detail as to who those other teams are.

Bloomberg were also privy to a note shared with developers at Haven Studios from executives Sean Decker and John Doyle that follows a recent test of the game: "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set. Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

Sony have, notably, failed to capitalise on the live service trend; I'm sure I don't need to remind you about Concord. Hell, this isn't even taking the end of Destiny 2 into consideration, once a driving force of live service games, or how Marathon has struggled to pick up an audience in the way that Sony may want it to. You just can't force a game to be popular, especially in a genre like shooters.

For those that either missed or forgot about Fairgame$, it was announced back in 2023 and was supposed to be a "competitive modern heist game where you team up to break into exotic locations and steal the cargo," all while taking on security and other, real people. Gameplay was never formally revealed, only a CGI trailer, and was set to come to PC as well as PlayStation. Bloomberg also noted that the game had been reworked multiple times since the announcement and was set to be re-revealed with a new name. Ultimately, it looks like Katharine was a little generous with her timeline of six months.

#3905. Girls und Panzer: All-Star Tank Carnival adds PS5 and PC versions, launches March 25, 2027 in Japan

Tank battle action Girls und Panzer: All-Star Tank Carnival will launch for PlayStation 5, Switch 2, and PC via Steam on March 25, 2027 in Japan for 6,980 yen, D3 Publisher announced. A limited edition will also be available for 14,080 yen. The PlayStation 5 and Switch 2 versions will be available physically, with the Switch 2 version shipping on a game-key card. The PlayStation 5 and PC versions are newly announced. Cross-play is supported between all three versions.

With the goal of further promoting tankery, the town of Oarai, home to Oarai Girls’ Academy, becomes the stage for a major event. Gathered in the festive town are all the rival schools that Miho and her friends have fiercely battled and built bonds with. The “Special Interleague Match,” which involves the entire town, is set to be held. Miho and her friends can freely roam the town, which is buzzing with festivities, enjoying lively interactions with their rivals and heated tankery battles.

Explore Oarai as Miho Nishizumi and Enjoy an Original Story

Players can control protagonist Miho Nishizumi and freely explore the familiar town of Oarai as seen in the anime. By talking to the other tankery girls scattered throughout the town, players can trigger game-original stories that naturally lead to heated tankery battles. Additionally, players can take commemorative photographs with their favorite characters via Photo Mode. Enjoy a virtual tour of Oarai while progressing through a new story!

Featuring Characters, Tanks, and Maps from Up to Girls und Panzer das Finale: Part IV

The game features characters and tanks from the TV series through the anime film Girls und Panzer das Finale: Part IV. Experience thrilling and immersive tank battles that take full advantage of the terrain, from aquatic combat navigating jungle waterways in the “Special Type 2 Launch Ka-Mi,” to snow battles fought while sliding across vast snowy fields.

Over 90 Characters! All Conversation Scenes Feature New Artwork

All of the conversation scenes throughout the game feature entirely new character artwork. Over 90 tankery girls engage in conversations with a wide range of expressive facial expressions. These dream interactions, which bring together characters from different schools, are a must-see for fans.

Online cross-play is supported across all three platforms. Enjoy heated tankery battles with up to 10 players, regardless of which platform they’re playing on!

Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang allegedly had an "intimate relationship" with a second Nvidia employee, according to Reuters.

This new allegation comes after Huang's resignation yesterday, following his admission of an affair, believed to be with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, and a New York Times report of another extramarital affair with Nvidia VP Kimberly Powell.

Reuters has chosen not to name the second Nvidia employee in question, but says the information comes from "two people familiar with the matter."

Huang's resignation from Nvidia came as a shock to many yesterday, marking a change in leadership at the top of one of the world's most valuable companies, and the fall of a key figure at the heart of the AI boom.

Huang has been replaced by an interim CEO at Nvidia, previous chief financial officer Colette Kress. The company's share price has since shown signs of recovery since the announcement of his departure, after dropping considerably during the tumult caused by the initial allegations, and the uncertainty regarding Huang's future at the company.

It's understood that the ex-Nvidia chief is scheduled to appear before the Senate Banking Committee alongside US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick in the coming weeks, regarding concerns over national security in relation to the initial allegations.

Riot Games has properly revealed League of Legends: New Dawn, the next big evolution of the long-running MOBA that's coming next year.

Announced during the 2026 League of Legends World Championship, New Dawn is said to be a sweeping update to the 17-year-old game that'll touch up everything from the gameplay to the client and much more.

"The client, for one, has to be better," executive producer Paul Bellezza said during the reveal. "So, next year, we're releasing a modernized client." The last time Riot Games overhauled League's under-the-hood architecture was a decade ago in 2016, so a technical dust up is very much welcome.

"But a client isn't enough. We're updating a lot," senior vice president and studio head Andrei van Roon chimed in. New Dawn is supposedly "visually revamping Summoner's Rift, evolving its gameplay, and adding new ways to play and experience your favorite champions."

"We want League to stand the test of time and be a game that's here for many years to come. And there are a lot of things that need to be true to make that happen," van Roon added.

We also got a pretty good look at LoL: New Dawn through both gameplay snippets and gorgeous cinematic shots of several champions, including Riven, Ahri, Jhin, Sett, Poppy, Lux, Blitzcrank, Leona, and Volibear.

Details are understandably light for now, but Riot plans to properly lift the lid early next year. A full blown League of Legends: New Dawn reveal is scheduled for January, 2027, according to the studio.

#3902. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang under investigation after admitting affair with alleged Chinese spy in company-wide email

"There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

Nvidia's board of directors has launched an investigation into its own CEO Jensen Huang, after a report by the New York Times claimed he had been participating in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to having an affair in a company-wide statement, apologising to his wife as well as to Nvidia employees. Following this acknowledgement, independent investigators are looking into whether or not he's been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort".

Per the New York Times article, the alleged spy was named as Megaspeed executive and Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang or Huang Le. Jensen Huang wrote in his internal letter: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

With regard to security concerns surrounding the CEO of US-based company Nvidia potentially sharing information with a spy, Huang confirmed that the Nvidia board of directors had initiated an investigation. He added: "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully." The Nvidia board has said it has "no reason to believe either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised."

Huang will remain CEO of Nvidia while the investigation is conducted. The New York Times report also claimed that US government officials did not believe Huang knew of Alice Huang's alleged intelligence activities for China.

Following the internal letter from Jensen Huang, Nvidia stock took a tumble from $162bn to $150bn. Nvidia, a juggernaut in the video game hardware industry, is also a key player in the global generative AI industry, which is currently carrying the US economy as other sectors struggle. The company is responsible for AI technology like DLSS 5, which generates lighting, shadows and more using generative AI.

Concerns around the Chinese AI sector passing the American industry has been a core argument against AI development slowdown or regulation, and it's also why Huang's affair may be a matter of national interest.

I reported earlier this week on a bug within AMD's GPU driver suite, wherein a misfiring utility was accused of making huge amounts of erroneous storage writes. Some AMD graphics card owners reported their SSD health dropping by up to 1% per month, but a fix has finally arrived.

AMD Adrenalin Edition 26.11.1 is an optional update, which means you'll need to download the installer yourself. However, according to the topline notes, the update fixes "excessive writes to the system drive" at idle for Radeon RX 7000-series graphics cards and above.

AMD's wording suggests that older GPUs might not be affected by the bug, but some of the user reports mention RX 6000-series cards, so it's unclear if a fix for earlier models is still in the works.

I also think it's a slightly odd move to make this an "optional" update, given the severity of some of the reports, though this is often how AMD deals with getting fixes out in between official driver releases—by the looks of the known issues, this interim driver might still need some work before it's patched into the next full release.

AMD lists a litany of potential issues with various games, including crashes and driver timeouts in Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, War Thunder, and Cyberpunk 2077 with FSR enabled. These issues, however, match and are fewer than in the previous driver release, with the exception of the Phantom Blade Zero bug.

The company notes that "visual corruption may appear on character hair while playing Phantom Blade Zero on Radeon RX 9000 series graphics products." I'm currently working my way through PBZ myself, and the idea of turning down the quality settings on Soul's magnificent hairdo? Sacrilege, as far as I'm concerned.

Still, I'd definitely consider downloading the update if my SSD health was rapidly being eaten by a misfiring utility. Buying a replacement these days isn't cheap, so anything that prevents unnecessary wear and tear on existing hardware is a-okay with me.

#3900. Sick BMX flips, colourful characters, a whole lot of mail and a charming raccoon dog await you in Tanuki: Pon's Summer, which you can pick up now

Right, today's been miserable thanks to the now hourly discourse we have to all take part in lest we be seen as approving of the current bad thing, how about something that looks simply pleasant? Today's the launch day for Tanuki: Pon's Summer, a delightfully vibrant mail delivery sim/Tony Hawk's Pro Skater but for bikes about restoring a shrine before the end of summer.

I've been enamoured by the vibe of Tanuki: Pon's Summer since it was announced in no small part because of how in some small ways it reminds me of Boku No Natsuyasumi, a cult-classic, Japan-only game series that's mostly just about hanging out in the Japanese countryside. This one isn't so lackadaisical, as you do have a job to do in delivering mail, but I think a similar spirit is there.

When it comes to delivering mail, there is a Death Strandingian element to it in your need to place your boxes on your BMX (which you can do sick tricks and flips on, of course) to maximise how much you can deliver. A bit less stressful than Kojima's joint, obviously, though elements are still there. Any money you earn from this gig can then be spent on restoring the shrine that you oh so love, which falls onto the sim side of things with the ability to fully customise how the shrine looks.

There are also a whole heap of minigames to perform that helps you get to know the locals. I'm talking baseball, sumo wrestling, working in a sushi restaurant and, of course, fishing. You can see bits of that in the launch trailer above, which comes with as 2010s an anime opening song you could wish for with some animation so good it makes me want an adaptation of the game. In time, perhaps! You can pick it up on Steam right here.

#3899. Strategy RPG Guild Saga: Vanished Worlds coming to PS5 in May 2027

Ontario-based developer Ocelot Technologies will release strategy RPG Guild Saga: Vanished Worlds for PlayStation 5 alongside its full release for PC via Steam in May 2027, the developer announced.

Guild Saga: Vanished Worlds first launched in Early Access for PC on October 10, 2024.

“We’ve been very happy with how much our audience has embraced Guild Saga: Vanished Worlds throughout its Early Access era, but we’ve always dreamt of bringing it to consoles, where our love of the genre first began,” said Ocelot Technologies CEO Mike in a press release. “PlayStation is the perfect place for Guild Saga, as we were massively inspired by the JRPGs that have long made PlayStation such a titan in the industry. Having it available on [PlayStation 5] feels like a homecoming, so we can’t wait for PlayStation fans to set sail to the Respite Archipelago in May!”

Here is an overview of the game, via lead developer Yasser Saleem on PlayStation Blog:

Create your hero’s appearance and choose their background, talents, and skills.

We wanted character building to leave room for creativity and experimentation. The progression system lets you combine skills across disciplines freely, as opposed to a more rigid class system. Skills let you deal damage, heal allies, change the environment, reposition across the battlefield, summon creatures, and alter the turn sequence. With hundreds of items, you can shape both your character’s build and their appearance, choosing gear that suits your playstyle and the look you want.

Your companions offer more opportunities to shape the party. Each brings a distinct history and personal quests, while their equipment, abilities, and attributes can be completely customized.

Through dialogue and shared experiences, you’ll discover more about the companions you choose to bring along. Friendships and romance can become part of your journey, giving you connections to your party members beyond the battlefield.

Guild Saga: Vanished Worlds features tactical turn-based combat with approximately 200 skills across ten disciplines. Express your tactical creativity by exploring how skills across different schools work together and with the environment around you.

Surface interactions and weather are an important consideration in combat. Players will need to be mindful of how surfaces interact, how weather affects the battle, and how those conditions might alter their skills.

For example, a party member with points invested in Geomancer may summon a mandrake to join the fight. A companion with Hydromancer skills can then make it rain, watering the mandrake and causing it to grow into a more formidable force. A party member with Aeromancer skills may then use lightning to electrify the puddles, paralyzing anyone standing in them. Across three disciplines, you’ve summoned an ally, strengthened it through the weather, and turned the resulting surfaces into a tactical advantage. We want players to discover combinations like this and experiment with how their party’s abilities work together.

Preparation matters too. Looting, mining, and gathering herbs provide materials you can craft into weapons, equipment, arrows, potions, and food. Whether you’re replenishing supplies or crafting new gear for a companion, taking time to explore and gather resources can help your party prepare for the next battle.

When designing exploration, we wanted players to feel that taking their time could lead to something worth finding. The main quest gives your journey direction, but the islands also invite you to wander, speak to NPCs, and investigate what catches your attention.

You might find yourself solving a murder mystery, hunting feared monsters for bounty money, or settling a deadly dispute between farm animals. Elsewhere, you can follow the imagination of a famed explorer or uncover an alchemical conspiracy. These side quests give you reasons to get to know the archipelago’s inhabitants and become involved in their troubles, whether sinister, strange, or absurd.

We wanted that variety to make following a new lead feel exciting. A conversation that seems like a small diversion can draw you into a story with its own characters, conflicts, and discoveries. Taking a detour is an opportunity to experience another side of the world and the people inhabiting it.

Hidden treasures, puzzles, valuable crafting resources, and unexpected encounters also reward exploration. Ancient books and forgotten notes offer glimpses into the world’s past, giving curious players more to uncover along the way.

We’re looking forward to welcoming PlayStation players into Guild Saga: Vanished Worlds when it launches on PlayStation 5 in May 2027. We’ll share the exact release date closer to launch.

From scrappy underdogs to successful Wardogs

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

To get into the game industry – at least at the level he’d always dreamed of – Joe Brammer had to tell a lie. In 2014, just as he was about to graduate from university, he applied for what was then the brand-new ID@Xbox scheme, which enabled novice developers to pitch to Microsoft in the hope of receiving an Xbox One development kit and a subscription to Unreal Engine. “I’d wanted to make games since I was 11, modding Battlefield,” Brammer says. “So I lied on the form, saying I’d worked for loads of people, like Lionhead. It’s funny when you look at that list of the first ID@Xbox studios now: CryTek, Sumo Digital, me.”

Working with a team of friends from his course, Brammer would co-create a firstperson Myst-style puzzler called Pneuma: Breath Of Life. “If we launched it today, we’d get slaughtered,” he continues. “It’s awful. But it was the first Unreal Engine 4 game on Xbox One, so Epic put us in all their booths”. Helped along by that whirlwind exposure, the game made about £400,000 in its first six months, more than enough to get production going on a new project. It also incentivised the formal founding of Bulkhead as a studio.

From a variety of fleetingly occupied offices around Derby (“We’ve moved about ten times by now,” Brammer says), the expanded and newly rebranded team would go to work on its next game, a follow-up first-person puzzler called, with an almost hubristic pragmatism, The Turing Test. Just like getting accepted into the ID@Xbox scheme, when it came to Bulkhead’s masthead debut, the ends were more important than the means, and what mattered above all was the will to get things done. “We basically made the whole game in white box, with about 100 puzzles,” Brammer recalls. “Then we went to a local college and we added a little popup at the end of each puzzle asking people to rate the difficulty and how much they enjoyed it. And then we put them in that order, on a spaceship. Honestly, it was easy.”

But if Bulkhead had been unfailingly confident up until now – and had grown to be much more successful, much more quickly, than its founders had ever anticipated – the studio’s next game would bring its surging momentum to a near-terminal stop. During development of The Turing Test, team members had taken to spending their lunchtimes playing competitive rounds of Call Of Duty 2 and Splinter Cell: Blacklist. Inspired by this older generation of multiplayer shooters – and deciding that they were, in Brammer’s words, “bored” with the puzzle genre – the team at Bulkhead started work on Battalion 1944, a World War II FPS that would pluck on players’ nostalgia for old-school COD. “But because it was a ‘classic shooter’, it just didn’t have any long-term retention,” explains UI and UX designer Howard Philpott. “We delivered,” Brammer continues. “We made an old-school shooter that reminds you of that era of games. But nobody wants to play that for more than three hours.”

Beyond the lack of long-term appeal, Battalion faced other, more immediate problems. After a highly successful Kickstarter, Bulkhead had once again partnered with Square Enix, its publisher for The Turing Test. Owing to a well-targeted pre-launch campaign, the studio had managed to push Battalion to the very top of the Twitch viewership charts – “We had some of the biggest streamers playing our game,” Brammer remembers. Ultimately, however, being one of the most watched games in the world would only serve to make the collapse of Battalion more spectacular, and leave an even bigger bruise on Bulkhead’s soul.

“We were using this thing for the backend called Google App Engine,” Brammer says. “It wasn’t really designed for what we were using it for, but in the alpha and beta test, it had been fine. On release day, though, once we hit 12,345 players, it all went down. Turned out, a Google programmer had just put in an arbitrary limit on users – someone at Google had gone, ‘Ah, just put in a limit, whatever – 12345’, so when we hit that number, it crashed. If they’d put ‘123456’, it would have been fine.”

“So we’re there phoning Google,” Philpott continues, “trying to find out what’s going on, and all the time we’re also watching TimTheTatman streaming the game. ‘Oh my god, TimTheTatman is streaming the game, and he can’t get into the server’.”

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

While Pneuma and The Turing Test had helped to put it on the map, and given shape to a dogged and strident work ethic – almost a bravura – that would remain at the core of its collective personality, Battalion would be the game to really define Bulkhead as a studio. “We were 24 at the time,” Brammer remembers. “We were saying, ‘We’re ready to release it’. But the adults in the room probably should have said, ‘Yeah, we need to delay it another six months’. It was a huge scar for us. It knocked our confidence. It’s why you haven’t heard of us until Wardogs. But then you don’t get Wardogs without us making the mistakes on Battalion.”

Despite learning some tough lessons from its first attempt at a shooter, Bulkhead’s route back into the genre – and to creating its most successful game to date – would be far from straightforward. After releasing Battalion, the studio was approached by Splash Damage with an offer to work on the infamously troubled, and eventually cancelled, Transformers Reactivate. Some time later, in December 2022, Splash Damage would buy Bulkhead outright. It was a close and affectionate relationship. “They always protected us from businesses and publishers,” Brammer says.

But a complication was on the way. Under Splash Damage, Bulkhead had already begun work on the prototype version of Wardogs. However, when Splash Damage’s parent company, Tencent, sold Splash Damage in 2025, it also negotiated a deal whereby it would keep Bulkhead. This transference of ownership – inheriting these new overseers – had never been part of Bulkhead’s plan. And so Brammer was suddenly rushing around, reaching out to potential partners and investors, trying to find a way to buy back the studio that he’d co-created. “I remember saying to people, ‘If you have another job offer, please take it’. And they were saying, ‘I believe in you, Joe. You can get it done’. I was like, ‘I’m telling you, we’re going to die!’ I was trying to kick people out but they just wouldn’t go.”

Those few months were arduous, but ultimately, in December 2025, the buyback was completed successfully. Less than eight weeks later, Bulkhead announced Wardogs. “For a British studio to make an FPS game of this scale, it’s a big deal,” Brammer says now. “I went through the British game-development education system, from college to university to making our own studio. I’m quite proud of that.” Now in early access, to a certain extent Wardogs’ success speaks for itself: since arriving on Steam in September, it’s sold over three million copies and maintained an average concurrent player count of more than 200,000. For Brammer, however, the game also illustrates the efficacy of Bulkhead’s studio culture. He makes no secret of the fact that Bulkhead expects its staff to crunch. More than that, he says that certain attitudes, perhaps more common in today’s videogame industry than in the past, are unlikely to fit in with the company’s practices and beliefs.

“We liked how talent-driven the industry used to be,” Brammer says. “And then it started to be about, ‘Everyone should be able to get a job in games’. We don’t really think like that. The floodgates opened, but now they’re closing again, and there might be some benefit to saying to people: ‘You have to be fucking good to be here, and you have to prove your worth’.

“Our team doesn’t love working late, but they do work late and we do crunch. What we’re saying is that sometimes, yes, life is more important. But sometimes, when you’re on the eve of releasing a game that keeps you all employed, work’s more important.” The more Brammer talks about Bulkhead’s ways of working, the more emphatic he becomes about the virtues of those expectations. “My mum was a teacher and a headteacher at a school,” he says. “I’ve never seen someone do so much crunch for barely any money. And so when game devs are like, ‘I don’t want to work overtime for my 100K salary’? Fuck. Off. Respectfully, it’s Californian bullshit.”

With regard to Wardogs itself, Brammer believes that the game has been aided by a certain creative absolutism. “A lot of modern business books will say, ‘You want to make sure everyone’s got a voice’, but I think that’s complete bullshit when you’re in a creative endeavour. You want to make sure everyone is heard, but that’s not the same as everyone has a voice.”

Despite this somewhat centralised approach to making games, Philpott says Bulkhead’s developers will often work across multiple areas of Wardogs. “Everyone has done something that’s not in their job description,” he says. “Everyone wears multiple hats, because they can see the path to success with the product.” In return, Brammer says that Bulkhead offers its staff a variety of bonuses and the opportunity to own shares in the company. With the early-access launch of Wardogs behind it, everybody at the studio will also be going on leave for the entire month of December. “We’re going to make sure players know they can fuck off in December,” Brammer says, laughing. “Go play GTAVI. We need to detox.”

As for Bulkhead’s next steps, there are plans to open a new office in Manchester and also to make – in Brammer’s words – “more games using our FPS technology”. But both he and some of the studio’s other senior figures are also thinking about the future in more philosophical terms. At the very top of its website, Bulkhead provides what is both its company motto and its ostensible mission statement: ‘The next big shooter studio’. Having finally released Wardogs, and seemingly cemented its place among the heights of the FPS genre, there is, for Brammer, a sense that this era of Bulkhead is complete – that the studio can now become something beyond what he’s been building for the past decade.

“We’re keen for people who are juniors and mid-level to step into leadership, so the old guard aren’t always running it,” Brammer concludes. “I mean, I guess just by default we’re a big shooter studio now. But I also don’t think that’s what we were really ever chasing. The best thing we can do is put Bulkhead in a position where it doesn’t require us.”

#3897. Anticipated Warhammer 40K tactical RPG Dark Heresy gets a release date

Owlcat Games has revealed a release date for its tactical role-playing sequel Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy. The game arrives 28th January, 2027 on PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S/X. A Switch 2 release date will be provided "at a later date", a press release says.

Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy follows the good work laid down by Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader a couple of years ago. "Rogue Trader nails the 40k setting and provides an appropriately massive narrative filled with meaty tactical combat, though some bugs and poor performance hold it back," wrote Caeyln Ellis in Eurogamer's Warhammer 40,000 Rogue Trade review.

Dark Heresy changes things by casting you as an Inquisitor and tasking you with hunting down heretics and purging the world of dark influences, as one is wont to do in the 41st century, it seems. And developer Owlcat has apparently overhauled many of the systems underpinning the adventure.

There's a beta that's been running for a while that offers a complete first Act to try, and it's accessible if you buy a Founders edition of the game. This beta, incidentally, disappears 7th January, when Owlcat prepares the game for launch.

Meanwhile, Owlcat is making a substantially different RPG based around the popular Expanse license - a game that's much more closely inspired by Mass Effect. That project recently recruited the help of former Dragon Age writer David Gaider, and it will no doubt hope to fill a much-lamented hole created recently by the cancellation of Mass Effect 5.

That's reportedly one quarter's profits for the bank.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI-enabled hacking is only continuing to get more impressive, and more scary, as a French bank claims a hacking group has cost it €100,000,000 (around $110,000,000)—about one quarter's profits. So not much, then?

That's according to an interview with Julien Carmona of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa with the AFP, which Boursorama reported. Carmona detailed the hack in an interview, claiming it to be a "heist of a new kind", stating the company has the "dubious honor of being the first French bank, and I believe the first European bank, to be the target of a successful fraudulent attack." (machine translated).

Carmona says the hack is "unprecedented in terms of sophistication" and "technicality".

Effectively, the hacking group managed to create fake IBANs, including those from Fortuneo (a bank owned by the group), "to trigger payment orders from Crédit Mutuel Arkea's own account to external parties using instant payment systems". These, "by definition have fewer controls than on classic transfers."

Carmona did clarify to Les Echos that though they use Fortuneo IBANs, "Fortuneo's system, and therefore its customers, were not affected."

‼️ AI-enabled hackers pulled about €100 million out of French bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account.Its chair, Julien Carmona, told AFP how. The attackers took material from a hacked supplier, used it to get into the bank and generated fake IBANs at its online bank Fortuneo.… pic.twitter.com/fduRERezPWNovember 13, 2026

Reportedly, the hacking group used a compromised service provider of some kind to get privileged access, thereby bypassing restrictions normally in place to stop this kind of hack. When asked by Les Echos why they didn't reveal the name, Carmona said, "This is a collective decision by the banks. This information is not in the public interest and could harm the security of the banking sector. Similar service providers could then be targeted."

Starting on Sunday, November 1, the hacking group apparently made sure "everything was done to circumvent controls, to make these illegitimate transfers appear legitimate."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

They then transferred the funds to legitimate European banks, where they then took that money and spent it on crypto platforms. This hack wasn't spotted until Tuesday, November 3, when access to the bank's information system was cut off, but by that point the damage was done.

The French bank has since brought in crypto specialists, who reportedly spotted the abnormal transaction on Sunday and Monday "But, at that time, they themselves, and no one to my knowledge, made the link with Crédit Mutuel Arkea".

Carmona says the hacking organisation was "a very well-organised, very well-equipped criminal group" and "very likely aided by advanced artificial intelligence."

It's not yet clear what role AI played here, but it's particularly good at analysing data, and of course has found value in coding over the last year. AI was only recently used by a cyberhacking gang to target 60 firms a few months ago. In this Korean case, though, the gang only managed to make $210 in ransom payments before being caught.

In that time, he has covered the latest doodads, contraptions, and gismos, and loved every second of it. Hey, it’s better than writing case briefs.

#3895. Keeping hold of Company of Heroes was essential for Relic to leave Sega, Relic CEO says – "Without it we would have been a dead studio"

In the nearly 30 years since they opened their doors, Relic have been an enormously influential studio. Responsible for lauded RTS series Homeworld, Dawn of War, and Company of Heroes, they also dabbled in other genres with third-person shooter The Outfit and the original Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine. Yet, despite this history, in 2024, when Relic were negotiating their sale from Sega to UK investment firm Emona Capita, CEO Justin Dowdeswell knew the rights to Company of Heroes had to be part of the deal. "Without it we would have been a dead studio," he tells me.

Without naming names Dowdeswell points out that there are "numerous examples" of studios that weren't able to survive on their name alone. Not only did Relic need the ability to make more games in the series that they were known for, but they also needed the income from back catalogue sales a series like Company of Heroes provides.

Dowdeswell joined Relic shortly after Sega acquired the studio in 2013. This was in the immediate aftermath of publisher THQ's bankruptcy auction, where studios and franchises were sold off to the highest bidder. While Sega bought the studio, they didn't buy the licenses to everything Relic had created. "The other games that Relic made – Homeworld, Impossible Creatures, The Outfit... formative games in many people's memory – they were all split up, scattered," Dowdeswell says. "I think that was... I won't say a tragedy, but it's unfortunate because Relic is the home of those games. It would have been great for them to stay with the studio."

Just as a hint of the messy history of acquisitions and auctions: this year we see Dawn of War 4 coming from studio King Art Games and published by Deep Silver. Deep Silver are a subdivision of Plaion, formerly called Koch Media, which was acquired by Embracer Group back when they were called THQ Nordic. Not that they were actually the THQ that originally published Relic's Dawn of War, Nordic Games renamed themselves THQ Nordic after they bought the THQ trademark at auction.

As for Homeworld, Borderlands developer Gearbox picked up the license to the sci-fi RTS in the bankruptcy auction, then contracted Blackbird Interactive's support on the remasters, before handing the latter lead development on Homeworld 3. That chain of events does have a more clear throughline to Relic's past however, as Blackbird was created by two of Relic's co-founders Rob Cunningham and Jon Aaron Kambeitz. (Speaking of studios struggling without the series they made their name with, Blackbird was on the verge of bankruptcy before Gearbox got in touch with the Homeworld work. So we very nearly existed in a world where they never got to make the brilliant Homeworld: Deserts of Kharak and Hardspace Shipbreaker.)

None of this is intended to be a knock on Dawn of War 4. From what I've played it's a very good Warhammer 40K RTS, if it perhaps sticks a little closely to the model laid down by Relic's original. What do I know, though, talking about their own games, Dowdeswell tells me that while "one of the messages to the studio is we can't just make [the same] things that we made 20 years ago and hope it goes well", re-releasing the 20-year-old Dawn of War sold very well for Relic and netted the team some very positive reviews on Steam. "There's a bit of a paradox there," he adds"

Anyway, this is all getting side-tracked. Back to holding onto Company of Heroes when separating from Sega. "Fighting for Company of Heroes when leaving Sega was crucial because I already lamented the fact that the other games didn't come with Relic," Dowdeswell says. "I couldn't really imagine a Relic where none of the games that the studio has made and was known for were any longer part of it."

Relic and new owner UK investment firm Emona Capital LLP were able to negotiate Company of Heroes as part of the sale from Sega and since then the studio has spent the past two years focusing largely on supporting the WW2 RTS and restoring their back catalogue. The most recent update is the massive 3.0 patch to mark the series' 20th anniversary. Which, among many changes, overhauls the Mediterranean-set RTS game's special effects, audio systems, NPC AI, and makes significant changes to the singleplayer grand strategy-inspired Italy campaign, as well as adding a whole set of autumn and winter-themed assets for community map makers. They've also released a series of DLCs adding new factions to Company of Heroes 3's skirmishes and multiplayer, re-released Dawn of War with a definitive edition and announced they're doing the same for the original Company of Heroes, along with Blackbird Interactive's help. Dowdeswell says foundation building masks a lot of the work going on behind the scenes: "We now self-publish all of this," he explains. "There were a number of things that we had to learn, skills we had to develop, capacity and capability that we had to build at the studio very, very quickly."

I ask if it was always the plan to focus on their back catalogue, or if they had plans to release new games. Dowdeswell says spending four years quietly working on a new game wasn't an option: "It's almost impossible to do it that way because of the current climate in the industry. We don't have a financial safety net." Though, the team do have larger ambitions. "We want to make new games, we want to provide a modern Relic game," Dowdeswell says. "That ambition to re-establish Relic as an innovator in this strategy space is a big part of what drives our creative direction on new games." Focusing on updating Company of Heroes 3, releasing DLC for the game, and making definitive editions of Dawn of War and the original Company of Heroes is what gets the studio to the place it can make a new game.

However, Dowdeswell resists any framing of Relic's work on Company of Heroes 3 as spinning their wheels or resting on their laurels while working toward a new game. He argues the game "sits in between" Relic's past and its future: "It's an established game that came out three years ago, but it's also a way for us to take some chances, experiment a little bit, and while doing that staying really closely connected to the players, That's what the idea was behind the updates because it was a way to have very quick iterations and touch points with players and provide, honestly, a way for us to fund everything in the future."

As to what Relic is making next, Dowdeswell wouldn't say. Though, he revealed trying genres besides real-time strategy was "almost a certainty", before adding "I don't think it's going to be a vast departure for where we are, so it will still be strategic gameplay. We're not going to go build a racer."

Team Meat has announced a new remake of its classic 2010 platformer: Super Meat Boy Again+, this time with a fresh coat of bloodsoaked paint and entirely new levels.

The brutally tough platformer became a cult hit more than a decade ago and spawned one sequel, one 3D spin-off and a whole speedrunning community dedicated to beating its masocore levels without dying. Super Meat Boy Again+ is more or less the same game, but with much more bolted on top.

"This version is just like the original Super Meat Boy game but with new art, music, cutscenes, levels, secrets and unlockables...new everything," the game's Steam page says. "Since 2010, millions of people [have] played Super Meat Boy, all the secrets are known, all the levels are mastered, all the characters unlocked, so we have to give fans familiar with the game something to pull their hair out over. That's the "+" in Again+, and no, we won't spoil it. You'll go into it blind like you did the first time you played Super Meat Boy."

Original composer Danny Baranowsky - better known as Danny B - is also back with an expanded soundtrack. The reveal trailer up above shows off how drastically different the game's updated art looks, too.

"For our old fans, we want to present the game as you remember it through the wonderful lens of nostalgia. For our new fans, we want to give you a great looking, easy to pick up but difficult to master platformer that you may have missed because it came out like 4 years after YouTube was invented," the studio explains.

There's no release date yet for Super Meat Boy Again+ and the only confirmed platform thus far is Steam.

#3892. Hollow Knight Silksong physical editions mention multiple "free content packs" incoming, and call Sea of Sorrow a "giant expansion"

More than a year after its initial release, physical versions of Hollow Knight: Silksong are finally arriving on players' doorsteps. It's the same brilliant and sometimes thrillingly cruel Metroidvania Eurogamer gave five stars to, except this time a pack-in booklet seemingly reveals the existence of multiple "free content packs" alongside the Sea of Sorrow DLC.

Hollow Knight: Silksong's physical editions were originally set to be delivered from 10th November, but some early handovers have given us a peek inside the box. Redditor Me_975 posted pictures of their Nintendo Switch 2 Edition, and there's a few interesting tidbits tucked away - most notably in the manual's chapter on Content Packs.

"The world of Hollow Knight: Silksong will expand with free content packs," the booklet reads. "Prepare for even more adventures filled with new friends, new abilities, and new ferocious foes!"

Developer Team Cherry confirmed plans for post-launch Silksong support last year, but remained pretty tight-lipped about what exactly that would look like. The indie outfit then announced the nautically themed Sea of Sorrow expansion, though we now have proper confirmation there's more content packs still to come, which shouldn't be a huge shocker considering all the free post-launch love Hollow Knight (the first one) received.

Speaking of Sea of Sorrow, that's mentioned here too: "In the first giant expansion, voyage across and beneath a salt-stricken ocean brimming with mystery and menace."

Sea of Sorrow's original release window was a vague 2026 - time's a-ticking, Team Cherry. Still no release date so far, but the booklet does say it's "Coming Soon." Of course, Team Cherry are quite infamous for working on games until they balloon wildly out of control. After all, Silksong was once upon a time intended to be a Hollow Knight DLC, but with games this detailed, I can't really complain about waiting a little extra.

If you are interested in owning Silksong physically, it comes with a big map of Pharloom and the rest of the booklet also includes some really lovely art seemingly ripped straight from the game, as well.

#3891. Casualties: Unknown is a total pain simulator that makes other survival games seem like massive cowards

Content warning for discussion of extreme violence and self-harm.

You haven't died in a videogame till you've died in Casualties: Unknown, a profoundly unwholesome cousin of Spelunky that simulates injury, infection and sensory distress with the same gusto Crusader Kings 3 reserves for papal politics. This is an intricate and imaginative celebration of pain - not merely an exacting survival game full of gauges to manage, but a laboratory study of just how many ways an animal body can feel, before it finally gives up the ghost.

I am one of a million canine hominids, created to undergo spectacular indignities by vicious human scientists, in a universe of suffering that spans several games from developer Orsoniks. I am the sorrowing vat-grown pup of a conclave of star-faring Dr Moreaus. My task is to collect... something, some gadget of great importance, from a cave on a deathly planet, located beneath three kilometres of booby-trapped and infested, poisonous and hateful rock.

Currently, I am trying to burrow into a sealed titanium drop pod with my bare paws, so that I can sleep somewhere warm. Too warm, in fact. The drop pod heaters feel like they were vindictively designed to discourage occupants from lingering, but I'm finding that dehydration is easier to address than hypothermia - there are pools of groundwater around that harbour only a slight risk of "minorly" fouling my intestines. So into the pod we go. After ripping away a layer of rubber, I smash some glass panes and promptly step in the fragments.

My computer screams, a hideous jangle of chords and static. The interface becomes a fritzing, flexing sphincter of pinks and reds. My punctured dogsbody flops and writhes, spurting yellow fluids and gobs of unintelligible text, ignoring my button inputs. They are my avatar no longer. They have been reduced to a squirming facet of the simulation's agony.

I gawp in guilt and terror at the status bar, now jammed with pulsing icons, then switch to my health display and determine that I am "bleeding catastrophically" from my right hind paw. I need to bandage that paw quickly. But first, I need to remove the glass. This takes the form of a 'minigame' in which I guide a shaking clawed hand with the cursor, hauling out shards even as my poor character threatens to pass out from the ordeal.

I've got two of five shards out when the earthquake kicks in. Already doubled over and delirious, my pioneering pooch is launched over the nearest cliff. They fall about 50 feet, rag-dolling off crags with a concussive whump, till they smash into a flooded wooden platform. The anatomical diagram on the health screen lights up like a wickerman. I don't appear to have broken any bones, but everything is hurting. What's more, I am soaking wet and hypothermia is taking hold, stretching blue veins through the clenching colours of my pain. The screen begins to look like some exotic, putrid flower.

Wringing my hands, I allow my mutant mutt about 10 seconds to recover from the shock of the fall, then open the health screen again and slowly tug out the last three shards of glass. It's actually easier than before, but not for the happiest of reasons: landing on my head appears to have numbed my senses. There will be longer term consequences, probably. Now I just have to bind the wound… except that I must have dropped my roll of gauze, while tumbling through the abyss. With sirens still flashing on the HUD, I peer about for a cave plant or other source of crafting materials. On the other side of the platform, I spy the corpse of another pitiful lab experiment. Perhaps there's a bandage in that huddle of clothes?

I hoist my sagging and babbling starpup to their feet, and limp over to investigate. Then I step on a pressure plate, and a six foot blade shoots up through my left thigh.

The screen is almost obliterated by crimson snow. The noise is... indescribable. I open the health screen again to assess the damage but I can't, because my dogperson has fallen into utter derangement. They want to be rid of their too-fruitful arteries, their stinking yellow blood. The clawed hand reappears, and I am forced to rake my own torso with it to regain access to the controls.

I am now gushing my life out from head to foot. Going by my plummeting heart rate, I have about 30 seconds to burn before I lose consciousness forever. I see no means of recovery, and I can't bear to watch my character bleed out. So instead, I detonate the chip embedded in their brain - the same chip responsible for the interface's rash of icons and warnings. According to the subsequent mission report print-out, my canine pioneer was feeling "dejected" when their head exploded.

The worst thing about the scenario I've just recalled is that it represents Casualties: Unknown at its least punishing. All of the above took place in the first of the game's 11 biomes - each procedurally generated, and 300 metres high - on the default "Tough" run setting. Resources are more plentiful up here, while active threats are fewer. There is scope to faff about and prepare - gathering plant matter for a crude woven bag, so I don't have to carry everything in my hands or mouth or tuck it into the folds of my body. There is time to crack open supply crates, and craft an implement of some kind.

The main danger, traps aside, is falling. Casualties: Unknown's terrain generator is not your pal. As regards the opening couple of biomes, at least, it works like a broken muck spreader, ejecting a mix of filthy clogs and particles that snag your jumps and often oblige you to dig through rock and gravel. You'll frequently be doing that in the dark, and even the smallest of exertions takes a perceptible toll – whimpers of effort, wheezing breath, double vision. The one major consolation is that you can wall-jump and slide down surfaces, a mocking touch of Prince of Persia.

Still, further down is where life gets truly unpleasant. There are sonic traps in certain biomes that cause brain damage and massive hemorrhaging. There are vast, rumbling insects you simply cannot afford to get close to, because they are guaranteed to bite off a limb. And the absolutely dreadful thing about that is that it won't necessarily end your run: given a tourniquet and antibiotics, you may yet pull through. Perhaps you'll find or craft a prosthetic. The game's characters are, in general, astonishingly tough for all their immense capacity for anguish.

Casualties: Unknown is a brilliant and unusual piece of design, uninhibited by any commercialised and sanitary notions of 'fun' and 'difficulty'. It's committed to recreating the surge of sensation through flesh. There's something intrinsically vital about this. Like Project Citadel, perhaps, its extravaganzas of torment are about feeling more present and alive in a twisted world, more in control. I'm not the writer to discuss this, and I know little about the developer's circumstances, but it feels like an exploration of trans survival in the face of a brutalising biopolitical regime: the online wiki notes that the game's zoomorphic Experiments or "Expies" have their own ideas about gender, though I'm finding it tricky to distinguish those accounts from the categorisations of the evidently unfriendly boffins who engineered them.

I would like to get to the bottom of things. I would like to find that goddamn gadget. I would like to return to the surface and massacre the bastards who sent me down here. Still, I'm not sure I have the willpower to witness everything my avatar might have to endure: barotrauma, sepsis, strokes, ruptured ears, hallucinations... As I've hopefully made clear throughout this piece, it remains an open question as to whether I am them, or simply one of their human tormentors. You can read more on Steam and Itch.

They threaten subpoenas if he doesn't show up, but he's intimated that he'll attend the meeting.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ex-Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang has again been summoned to United States Congress to speak with lawmakers. On the agenda are national security issues that may have arisen from his, and his company's, relationship with MegaSpeed, a Singaporean-registered company at the centre of a debate about China's access to high-performance GPUs; possible interference with US export control investigations; and chip smuggling.

“As reports continue to come to light regarding Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and Megaspeed, there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately,” US committee chairmen Mast, Moolenaar, and Crawford say about the letters summoning Huang, Nvidia's General Counsel Tim Teter, and Under Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler to Congress.

“We need to know the full extent to which our national security has been put at risk," the chairmen say.

This meetings are to take place with the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, House Select Committee on the CCP, and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. Huang and Teter's meetings are described as 'closed-door transcribed interviews', taking place on December 1 and December 2, respectively. Both parties are threatened with subpoena to force their attendance if they do not comply with the request. Under Secretary Kessler's invitation is described as a "hearing" and is much more amicable.

It's a marked change in tone for Huang compared to a letter sent by the chairmen prior to his resignation from Nvidia, which simply asked him to offer an alternative date should he not be able to attend. That focused more on Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy and former managing director of MegaSpeed.

The letter to Nvidia's counsel Teter outlines the more recent concerns of the committees:

"This letter is to request your appearance for a closed-door transcribed interview on December 2, 2026, regarding AI chip smuggling, adversary military use of Nvidia products, and recent public reports regarding Nvidia's interference in U.S. export control policies and investigations, including those involving MegaSpeed."

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

If that's not a big headache for Nvidia, its former CEO has also been called in for a hearing with the US Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs. This hearing is led by chairman senator Tim Scott.

Scott also calls on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to attend a hearing. Lutnick is Kessler's boss, and has reportedly accepted Scott's invitation. Lutnick has come under some scrutiny as to whether he was too soft on, or protected, Nvidia.

Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology. I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee. The American people deserve answers.November 13, 2026

And the democrats readying to take over Congress next year aren't happy with Huang, Nvidia or the supposed risks to national security, either.

There needs to be a full accounting of Jensen Huang, Nvidia, Megaspeed, and the Trump administration's actions in light of serious national security risks. We don't need to wait for Dems to take over Congress in January. At a minimum, Congress needs to be briefed immediately.November 12, 2026

Huang's hearing with the Banking Committee is set to be public, taking place on December 3. It covers the "significant national security concerns" raised by recent reports, according to the letter.

The BBC reports that Huang is willing to appear before Congress.

#3889. Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection announced for PS5, Xbox Series, Switch 2, PS4, Xbox One, Switch, and PC

Atari publishing label Infogrames and developers Graphite Lab and Implicit Conversions have announced Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection, a collection of seven Lucky Luke games from Game Boy Color, Super Nintendo Entertainment System, PlayStation, and Game Boy Advance. It will launch for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Switch, and PC via Steam on January 13, 2027.

Here is an overview of the collection, via Infogrames.

Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection brings seven Lucky Luke titles from the 8-, 16-, and 32-bit eras to all modern platforms for the first time.

Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection includes

Every game features quality-of-life improvements, including improved graphics, save states, achievements, visual filters, custom screen bezels, and rebindable controls. “How to Play” guides onboard unfamiliar players and help them solve difficult challenges.

The bonus Frontier Experience is an interactive first-person museum and shooting gallery that allows players to explore the history of the iconic gunslinger firsthand. Players can explore western locales, enjoy target-shooting minigames, search for collectibles and discover original comic and character art.

The legendary Lucky Luke originated in 1946 with a French-Belgian comic book about a street-smart gunslinger famous for shooting faster than his own shadow. Over the past 70 years the cowboy has gone on to feature in numerous comics, several animated television series, feature films, and most recently a 2026 live-action television series.

The Lonesome Cowboy Collection reunites Infogrames with the popular western franchise. Infogrames published several Lucky Luke titles in the late 90s and early 2000’s, including the incredibly rare Playstation Platinum edition of Lucky Luke: Western Fever.

The collection includes four games that were only released here in Europe and never made it to the United States, including the 1997 Super Nintendo Entertainment System release of Lucky Luke, the 2000 Game Boy Color release of Lucky Luke: Desperado Train, the 2001 PlayStation release of Lucky Luke: Western Fever, and the 2001 Game Boy Advance release of Lucky Luke: Wanted!

Overwatch's 55th hero is set to be Hudson, a cool robot detective who has a portion of the player base groaning with DPS fatigue. Game director Aaron Keller says he understands the disappointment, but the goal is always to release a "great character" rather than prioritizing role variety above all else.

Hudson was originally teased as an incoming support hero, but the Overwatch team recently revealed that the hero had pivoted into the damage role which already dominates the shooter's hero roster. Right now, the game has a whopping 23 damage heroes - versus 16 supports and 15 tanks. The revelation didn't go down too well with support and tank mains hoping for more variety.

Casefile Status: Declassified 🗂️ We can’t wait for you to meet the newest Damage Hero, Hudson, in Season 6! https://t.co/AWGVOrR7yyNovember 12, 2026

"We've seen a lot of discussion about the role (DPS) of the Season 6 Hero. We understand that you were looking forward to another Support Hero next season and I hope that giving context for the decision will help players understand it, even as some of them are disappointed," Keller says on social media.

"When we started work on the detective, he was a Support. But as time went on and the kit continued development we realized that it wasn’t working. Once we tested Hudson as a DPS, the turn around in our feelings for him was instantaneous and dramatic," he adds. "This decision ultimately wasn't whether we release a DPS or a Support hero, it was whether we release a great character or one we didn't believe in. Building Heroes for OW is as much of an art form as a technical challenge."

The Overwatch lead continued to explain that game development "isn't always straightforward," and in some cases the team needs to "adapt to create the best version of something." Blizzard is supposedly "incredibly proud" of how Hudson plays ahead of his introduction in Overwatch Season 6 this December.

This isn't the first time an Overwatch hero has slotted themselves into an entirely new role. Symmetra was once a support hero, before eventually finding her place as a DPS. Even more recently, hacker Sombra went from a damage hero to a support hero who can 'hotfix' her team. The change might have "upset" some Sombra mains, but the hero does admittedly work much better now.

#3887. As The Elder Scrolls 5 turns 15, massive mod Beyond Skyrim: Bruma gets a 2.0 update delivering a new quest, extra dungeons and an "expanded worldspace"

"The reason for this update is actually a technical necessity"

Warning: I'm probably about to make you feel old. Today, November 11th 2026, is the 15th anniversary of Skyrim's release. The first one, before it was re-released on every other platform under the sun. Fittingly, one of its best expansion mods, Beyond Skyrim: Bruma, has gotten a beefy 2.0 update to commemorate the occasion. Though, its creators insist the main driving force behind the update was more a matter of "technical necessity". There are new quests, dungeons, and corners of Skyrim-era Cyrodiil to explore either way.

"You might ask yourself why, after all these years, we have put any more work into polishing and even adding new content to Bruma," the Beyond Skyrim team wrote in an article about the making of their version of Bruma's 2.0 update. "We are, of course, working on the whole province of Cyrodiil, and have made significant progress which you can follow on our social media. With so much still to go however, it was not out of nostalgia for a 15 year old Skyrim or a nearly 10 year old Bruma that we decided to revisit the first, and as of the time of writing, only major Beyond Skyrim release.

"The reason for this update is actually a technical necessity," the modders continued. "The problem we have with Bruma is that it is based on a very very old version of Cyrodiil, which had been branched off of the main development build of Cyrodiil soon after Bruma's initial release in 2017. Whenever we updated Bruma, that meant we had to merge our changes into two builds, the public Bruma build and the WIP Cyrodiil build." So, in order to solve that behind-the-scenes problem, the team have developed a "build stripper" tool which means they'll not have to juggle maintaining two builds going forwards.

As laid out in the showcase video above, the modders have also used Bruma 2.0 as an opportunity to overhaul and add to vast chunks of their recreation of Cyrodiil's northernmost county. A fully voiced quest called All The Wrong Places which was cut from the mod's initial release, "several new dungeons and interiors", and an expansion of the explorable area all grace the changelog.

More clothing, armour, weapons including the mod's first spear, enemies, spells, enchantments, world encounters, books, and treasure maps have also been shipped in with the 2.0 version, alongside overhauls to boss fights. A new opening title splash will greet you upon entering Bruma for the first time, you should benefit from higher FPS as you explore the city, and the modders have even added an apple to Jerall View Inn. That's far from the end of the tweaks, so it's well worth reading the full list if you've got time.

"All in all, Bruma 2.0 has been a massive journey, one where we have built and learned a lot, and most importantly, made many advancements to prepare us for the future," the modders concluded. If you've not given Beyond Skyrim: Bruma a go, I can very much recommend it. You might find yourself wandering back across the border into Skyrim once you've had your fill of nostalgia-tinged exploration and staring at a distant Imperial City you can't visit, but the original version's still good for hours of extra Elder Scrollsing.

You can grab the 2.0 version of Beyond Skyrim: Bruma from Nexus Mods. It's worth noting that you'll need "a recent version (1.6 or higher) of Skyrim: Special Edition's update.esm and update.bsa" and a separate mod containing Beyond Skyrim's shared asset repository. Saves made using previous versions of Beyond Skyrim: Bruma won't work with the 2.0 update, so it's likely worth starting a new playthrough or relying on an in-progress one you've yet to use any mods with.
