#3886. God of War: Ragnarok is reportedly the highest-earning PlayStation Studios game this generation, but Marvel's Spider-Man 2 isn't far behind

God of War: Ragnarok is the generation's best-selling and highest-earning PlayStation Studios game, according to a new report, but the full top 10 list has a few nice surprises.

In the four years since its PS5 release and two years since its PC port, God of War: Ragnarok has reportedly sold just over 20m copies and generated $1.4b in revenue, according to estimates from Alinea Analytics. About 27.5 percent of the 15m copies it sold on console came from physical editions, and the action blockbuster apparently sold a further 1.1m this year alone. Not bad, boy.

Those stats should bode well for the series' next romp God of War: Laufey - which sees Faye take the spotlight across a multi-mythological afterlife and was recently delayed into May 2027 - even if PlayStation moves away from PC ports for its signature single-player games.

Kratos and Atreus only narrowly beat out perhaps the biggest superhero of them all: Marvel's Spider-Man 2, a game that reportedly made a whopping $1.3b off 19.1m copies across PS5 and PC. The Spidey sequel should keep swinging even higher as the years chug on, though - the report states that sales always surge during the holiday months, and this year's big screen behemoth Spider-Man: Brand New Day led to an even bigger spike than usual.

Racing sim royalty Gran Turismo 7 ($841m), bug-squashing phenomenon Helldivers 2 ($786m), robo-dino sequel Horizon: Forbidden West ($485m), vengeful spirit sim Ghost of Yotei ($410m), undead remake The Last of Us Part 1 ($341m), multidimensional romp Ratchet and Clank: Rift Apart ($334m), Stellar Blade ($316m) and delightful throwback Astro Bot ($292m) round out the top 10 games published by PlayStation Studios this generation.

It's worth noting that Helldivers 2 and Stellar Blade were developed by studios outside the PlayStation umbrella, but the console maker still published both upon release. Ghost of Yotei's performance is also particularly impressive since Sucker Punch's sequel has only been out for a year and didn't get the benefit of a PC port, like many of its PS5 siblings. The success couldn't save Sucker Punch from recent layoffs, however.

On PlayStation's decision to kill disc-based physical releases, analyst Rhys Elliott said that the bottom five games in the list together made $281.7m this year alone: "PlayStation wants those numbers to be bigger in the coming years, which is one of the reasons it's killing the disc (alongside the better margins it and publishers get through digital.)"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A couple of days ago I reported that Reddit is rolling out reviews for different products, informed by Redditors' thoughts and molded by AI into into dedicated review pages for these products. Given Reddit says "many reviews also include images, prices, and purchase links", I wondered whether Reddit would be making any affiliate money from this. Well, I now have an answer: the company tells us it will not receive a cut.

In an email sent to me, a Reddit rep explains: "Reddit Reviews is an organic experience, and Reddit does not receive a cut of any purchases made through the buy it now button on product pages."

Not that I would have had a massive problem with this—PC Gamer earns affiliate revenue itself—but I suppose it's good to know there won't be a financial incentive there at least in that respect. And it does at least tie in with the aimed "organic" nature of Reddit in general.

I was also concerned that users might review-bomb products they don't like, or that companies could use bots to positively influence reviews for their own products. Reddit reassures us about that, too:

"Platform-wide, we are taking numerous steps to prevent and enforce against inauthentic content."

That's certainly more reassuring than nothing, but we'll have to see how it goes in practice. AI and bot farms make the modern landscape tricky business, and I'm sure there must already be actors out there giving pretty convincing supposedly first-personal reviews of products on different platforms, whether to bolster or undermine these products.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

As always, the proof will be in the pudding (or rather, for the pedants, in the eating of it).

Reddit Reviews is rolling out to US iOS users and will cover around 10,000 products, but the company plans to add more products and expand to other locations throughout 2027.

#3884. The Outer Worlds 2's first story expansion could well be the opening to the series' last hurrah and will have you hunting for a cure to "explosive cell death" in December

Sub Rosa sci-fi drama and a new region to explore await

Since they released The Outer Worlds 2 around this time last year, the world has rather turned upside down for Obsidian. The studio lost a chunk of staff to Microsoft's mass layoffs and have pivoted to making a new Fallout game as a smaller group shoved underneath Bethesda in Xbox's corporate structure.

Given all that, The Outer Worlds 2's two-part story expansion is likely arriving in vastly different circumstances than those the studio might've imagined when they began sketching out DLC plans. Part one of the expansion, dubbed Side Effects Guaranteed, is set to release early next month.

'Oof, that looks a lot like it's been given what could turn out to be a death spot parked right in the aftermath of GTA 6's initial launch on consoles' is what I thought when I first saw that Side Effects Guaranteed's launch date is December 2nd. That said, Obsidian have also made clear that a second DLC in the two-part narrative expansion to the sci-fi RPG is set to follow in spring 2027. So if this does turn out to be the end of the series, with a third Outer Worlds game currently looking very unlikely following the substantial upheaval I mentioned in the intro, at least it won't risk being totally obscured by a Rockstar crime game-shaped eclipse.

As for what this first dose of extra Outer Worlds 2 has in store for December, Obsidian summed it up as follows:

As you pursue the cure and set course for Elysium, an area home to former subjects of base game authoritarian collectivist faction the Protectorate, you'll be faced with the choice of whether to side with Gordon Hazen or Algernon Lankester. Both are agents of black market smuggling organisation Sub Rosa, with one sounding like the goody-two-shoes diplomatic type and the other wanting to "exploit the subjects for his own personal gain". Sounds more Saturday morning cartoon than serious RPG story with serious choices, but that's always tended to be how The Outer Worlds leans.

Rounding out the expansion are new enemies, gear, flaws which give your character build a funky twist, and a bumping up of the level cap from from 30 to 36. Fittingly given I'm writing this on Skyrim's 15th birthday, one of the new flaws is named 'Must Have Been the Wind' after the meme of enemies in the likes of Bethesda and Obsidian's games returning to chill mode after being shot in the face with an arrow or facing some other obvious sign they're under attack. To encourage folks to dive back in, The Outer Worlds 2 is getting options to respec your character's skills and edit how many skill points are dished out per level up via an update alongside Side Effects Guaranteed.

As much as I'm resigned to the series' likely fate as Obsidian return to Fallout and won't pretend The Outer Worlds 2 was great rather than good, I'm still hopeful it can go out with a bang in these two expansions, if indeed this is the studio's last trip to space for the foreseeable future. It's worth noting that if you bought The Outer Worlds 2's premium edition, these expansions are included as part of it and so will come to you at no extra cost.

#3882. "Something's really possible" - Mass Effect cast rally around efforts to save the franchise on the first N7 Day after BioWare's closure

I'm Commander Shepard and this is my favorite video on the internet.

This N7 Day was the first without developer BioWare around, but fans of the Mass Effect series didn't let 7th November go by quietly. The community managed to get several notable Mass Effect actors to lend their voice to the increasingly loud 'SaveMassEffect' movement.

In the weeks since BioWare's shock closure and Mass Effect Universe's cancellation, the community-organised We Are Mass Effect group have put up billboards in Times Square, a mobile billboard outside BioWare Edmonton's former office and much more while directing attention to an online petition.

Today is a very special day for Mass Effect fans. We've worked incredibly hard to bring together most of the original Mass Effect trilogy's voice cast to share a very important message with you. We need to #SaveMassEffect. https://t.co/FOp0qp4wBI

And for the series' annual celebration, the group managed to get a sizable portion of the Mass Effect cast to join in. Commander Shepard actors Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer, original trilogy composer Sam Hulick, Garrus' Brandon Keener, Jack's Courtnay Taylor, Tali'Zorah's Ash Sroka, Thane's Keythe Farley and many more all showed up in a two-minute video to help potentially salvage the series - sometimes in character.

"When we heard about the formal closing of Boware, I felt weirdly hopeful," Hale said in a separate interview with IGN. "I can't explain it. I just got so weirdly hopeful. My first thought, of course, was for the devs and all the people. And then I just closed my eyes and crossed my fingers and I said, 'I feel something's possible. You know, something's really possible.'"

The other half of Commander Shepard, Mark Meer, noted that "this didn't all just happen in the last 10 days." Near yearly layoffs at EA had slowly trimmed multiple BioWare teams down, sometimes even affecting studio veterans who had been at the company for decades.

"A lot of senior writers within the last year or two were let go. People who had been there from the very beginning. Again, people who had built that company from the ground up, who built the bones of it, who made those games that had captured people so much right back from the 1990s," Meer said.

#3880. Lootboxes, pay-to-win, virtual currencies and other blights unto gaming face heavy regulation as the EU tables new Digital Fairness Act

It's been 10 years since I lasted opened a lootbox, I think. Just thought you should know.

Loot boxes, dark patterns, virtual currencies, subscription services, pay-to-win systems, and many other trappings of diabolical digital serfdom all face extensive regulation under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act, which has been formally presented to EU member states today. The full draft text of the regulation leaked earlier in the week. If it passes into law - and there's plenty of debate and revision ahead - it'll have big consequences for the developers and publishers of games like Overwatch, Dota 2, and GTA Online.

You can now read the draft text here on the EU Commission's official site. The organisers have also published an introductory explainer that takes us through the timeline of the Act's gestation, dating back to 2020, and summarises its provisions. If passed, the Act will apply to any company doing business in the EU, not just those based in member states, with individual governments able to impose fines and consumers able to seek financial compensation if they think they've been harmed.

Here's a summary from me, based on a quick delve through the text. The Act proposes a number of provisions regarding "unfair" commercial practices, including omission and distortion in advertising and PR communication at large. Amongst other things, it takes aim at "dark patterns" – that is, "visual, auditory and other components" of online interfaces that are designed to manipulate or deceive. The text also forbids personalised advertising and pricing aimed at children, and prohibits influencers from making "direct exhortations to minors to buy products or to persuade their parents or other adults to buy products in commercial communications".

The items that are probably of greatest interest to us smelly gamers are the passages on virtual currencies, "variable reward systems", and addictive design.

The Act would require game publishers who sell virtual currencies to indicate the real-world monetary value of the currency and anything bought with it. It would also require companies to disable paid-for virtual currencies by default for kids, unless a parent or guardian has given approval.

As for paid-for "variable reward systems", aka "loot boxes", "surprise mechanics", "Schrödinger's Giftbombs" or however publishers may prefer to describe them, the Act would require companies to state the "types" of object they might cough up, together with the probability of obtaining them. It would also oblige publishers to disable paid-for "variable reward systems" for minors, and give everybody an "easily accessible" way to switch them off.

The draft Act outright prohibits "pay-to-progress and pay-to-win mechanisms" for kids. More generally, it suggests further constraints for publishers and developers who "design, organise or operate their digital products in a manner that is intended, or can reasonably be foreseen to encourage compulsive or excessive use". Again, it wants companies to give people options to switch these features off.

That includes "features enabling automatic play of content and uninterrupted content consumption without effective and regular interruption moments that enable deliberation by the consumer on their willingness to consume more content". Also, "notifications not triggered by, or not directly related to, the consumer’s interaction or activity on the service", "features incentivising engagement at regular times or with greater frequency, including through penalties or loss of benefits", and "features and system behaviours that encourage continued use by simulating interpersonal relations," such as nagging prompts.

If you'd like a more 'expert' account of the Digital Fairness Act - how dare you! I have read several Wikipedia pages - the bespectacled nabobs of GamesIndustry.biz went and got notes from an actual lawyer. All this follows a change in EU rating law last month aimed at safeguarding the weans from predatory habit-forming devices and instruments of financialisation - games with lootboxes are now PEGI 16 by default, while blockchain games are always rated 18. Across the pond, meanwhile, lawsuits are underway in New York and Washington against Valve's tolerance of lootboxes on Steam, which the lawyers in question define as illegal gambling.

Ain't nobody buying gaming CPUs right now.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Intel appears to have gained market share from AMD in a rare turnaround for the company. The red team's chips have been in the lead in performance and popularity for many years now, and frankly, they still are. That's what weird about this one: AMD may have lost ground because it makes the best CPUs for gaming.

The latest Q3, 2026 data from market researchers Mercury Research suggests an increase in market share for desktop CPUs of 5.1%. Now, considering AMD has fought tooth and nail for a decade to increase its share to around 35% as of Q2, 2026, dropping down to just 29.9% in the following three months marks a gargantuan lurch back towards Intel.

Our pick for the best gaming CPU is the AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, and many other AMD chips make up our recommendations. While we do recommend the Intel Core Ultra 5 250K Plus due to its surprisingly low price tag and plenty of cores, I wouldn't go as far as believing any Arrow Lake chip has been key to turning around Intel's fortunes among gamers. The architecture struggles to keep up with AMD's latest in gaming, and it is built on a dead-end platform—Nova Lake chips are expected soon on a different motherboard socket.

The increase in market share is almost too big to be believed, which is certainly one theory as to what's going on. A rounding error or errant data—though Mercury Research have been pretty locked in in the past. Both Intel and AMD cite their numbers when it makes them look good.

Mercury Research put its hands up to say it isn't totally sure what happened, either:

"It's difficult to know the driver of this for sure, but we speculate that due to the lower mobile CPU demand, Intel could allocate more products to the desktop market, which normally sees a significant demand increase in the third quarter, and Intel had been under-supplying this market earlier in 2026.

"AMD, however, did not appear to have a seasonal increase, which resulted in Intel having a very large sequential and on-year gain in desktop CPU market share," Mercury Research says.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

The other theory presented by the market research company is that AMD has "greater exposure" to gaming—by way of offering the best gaming chips.

"We believe another component to Intel's gains here is AMD's greater exposure to the PC gaming market, which has suffered due to supply constraints of gaming GPUs."

Mercury Research say 'supply constraints' when it's more like prices are so absurd for GPUs, RAM, and storage as to be comical, which lends to a general malaise among gamers to building a new PC. But, either way, this theory makes some sense. Intel still holds huge sway with system builders and OEMs, the likes of which are buying up both new and old (DDR4-compatible) chips for cheap systems. And not just gaming systems, which we see both Intel and AMD get a fairly decent share of during our weekly trawling for gaming PC deals.

AMD also admitted it is has a supply deficit at the moment; demand is outstripping supply. It's working to close that deficit, but what it means by that is grow its datacentre chip business more in the coming months and years. After all, AMD is a datacentre company now.

I wouldn't mistake Intel 'gaining market share' as a healthy sign for the company or the wider industry. Mercury Research suggested desktop CPU volumes had seen a "large drop" in Q2, 2026, and both Intel and AMD are said to have seen more than a 10% drop in shipments for mobile chips in Q3, 2026. They're fighting for scraps in the consumer market.

Intel has seen a momentous share price drop as of late due to weak sale expectations due to a crappy PC market, but AMD is set to beat Intel for total revenue by the end of year.

#3877. GTA 6 pre-orders are tracking "well above expectations" and the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two, says CEO Strauss Zelnick

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick noted that pre-orders for Grand Theft Auto 6 are tracking "far above expectations", and is certain that soon "numbers will speak for themselves" when it comes to the game.

Zelnick also promised GTA Online and GTA 5 will continue to receive updates in order to support the "nearly 235 million" units sold to date across "an unprecedented three console generations". The GTA series as a whole has, to date, sold over 480 million units. Karl Statoff, president at Take-Two, adds the launch of GTA 6 will be a "defining moment for the company and global entertainment industry". Zelnick adds, later in a question and answer session, that he expects GTA 6 to "set a new baseline" for Take-Two. "The future's really bright across the board," he notes.

For the next quarter, Take-Two expects to deliver $3.35 billion to $3.5 billion - with "recurrent consumer spending" to raise by 12 percent, driven by "the groundbreaking release" of Grand Theft Auto 6, and expects to see "significant growth for the Grand Theft Auto series", driven by sales of - specifically - Grand Theft Auto 6's Ultimate Edition, which includes add-on content, and that most people are pre-ordering at its $100 price point. That bonus $20 between the $80 base edition and the Ultimate Edition is counted as "recurrent consumer spending", as is part of that massive bump the company has seen.

It also seems that we will see more GTA games - or content, at least - sooner than expected. "We do think that the nature and velocity of the content we'll see from our iconic franchises, including GTA, will look dramatically different over the next decade." It's a vague comment, but assumedly the work done on the engine and backend of GTA 6 means we'll see more content arriving in shorter order than we're used to for the series. This is per an article published by IGN in line with the earning's call going live.

Elsewhere in the earnings call, Take-Two referred to its current setup with its mobile, sports, 'core new IP' and 'core existing IP' as "the strongest development pipeline in the company's history". In terms of new IP, Zelnick directed investors to consider the launches of incoming projects like Ken Levine's mysterious Judas and Project Ethos (which we don't know too much about yet, other than it's billed as a "roguelike hero shooter"). For core IP, 8 sequels and 7 remakes, remasters, and platform extensions.

Buoyed by these plans, Zelnick outlines that he believes that fiscal year 2027 "will be a historic year for Take-Two" as the company is buoyed by "recent and upcoming releases". No prizes for what that's referring to. If you're curious about what sort of numbers we may be looking at here, all you need to do is cast your mind back to 2014, where you will remember GTA 5 made $1bn in just three days.

#3876. "Some of the best games of the last decade came from teams of fifty": Destroy All Humans! remake devs Black Forest Games split from THQ Nordic to launch new indie studio group

"We're excited to shape our own future as owners again"

Black Forest Games, developers of the Destroy All Humans! remakes, have spun out of Embracer Group-owned publishers THQ Nordic via a management buyout and announced plans to form a new "developer-driven group" of independent studios. The new group, dubbed Third Signal, will aim to "give teams the independence, resources and creative freedom" to "bring their own ideas to life".

Black Forest, based in Germany, announced the move in a press release. "We are grateful to THQ Nordic and Embracer for nine good years and the games we made together," co-boss Adrian Goersch said. "Now, we're excited to shape our own future as owners again, to work on an exciting new project with a great team and strong partners behind us."

Black Forest had been in the embrace since 2017, releasing both 2020's Destroy All Humans! remake and Destroy All Humans! 2: Reprobed in that time, plus DLC Clone Carnage. Over the years they've also made multiple entries in the Giana Sisters platformer series, survival game Fade to Silence, and 2017's Bubsy: The Woolies Strike Back.

That's a right old mix of stuff, but the biggest names in it are all resurrections of series or characters created by other folks back in the day. Pandemic Studios in the case of Destroy All Humans!, Accolade in the case of Bubsy, and Germany company Time Warp in the case of Giana Sisters. That makes the fact it sounds like this move'll give Black Forest a bit more creative freedom intriguing. Here's hoping that if they do plan to try and get some more of their own original ideas off the ground, rather than trucking on with a steady diet of remakes and revivals, they manage to stick the landing. It's all fine declaring that a 50 person team can make a top game these days, but that certainly doesn't mean it's in any way easy to pull off.

Over a decade ago, Hugh Jackman outlined his dream crossover between X-Men and Avengers. Now, Avengers: Doomsday is going to do right by that idea – and bring home 25 years of history between those characters.

"You see interviews of Hugh Jackman 15, 20 years ago saying, ‘People say it’s impossible, but maybe someday the X-Men and the Avengers can all get together,'" Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige told Empire. "It just felt right. It just felt like the fun way to culminate a quarter-century of storytelling."

When doing press for 2013's The Wolverine, Jackman mentioned on multiple occasions that he would love to go claw-to-claw with The Avengers.

At the time, he told Slash Film, "I actually just asked the other day, I said, 'I don't know what the legal situation is, but why don't these companies come together? Why isn't it possible?' Because personally, I would love to mix it up with Robert Downey Jr. and Iron Man and kick his ass."

For now, Hugh Jackman isn't officially part of Doomsday – though, curiously, has a writing credit alongside Ryan Reynolds, which partially suggests Deadpool and Wolverine will factor in somehow.

But there are plenty of X-Men to make up for it, including James Marsden's Cyclops, Sir Ian McKellen's Magneto, and the late Patrick Stewart reprising his Professor Charles Xavier role once more. Channing Tatum's Gambit is also featured, but with a slightly different accent to his incomprehensible Cajun drawl that was played for laughs in Deadpool and Wolverine.

#3874. As investors ask about GTA 6 and AI, Take-Two CEO once again puts faith in dev creativity, states making hit games "remains the purview of human beings"

"Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future."

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick fielded questions from investors after presenting the financial results of the company. One caller was concerned about AI - specifically about the proliferation of AI-powered compilations and decompilations that have been raising piracy concerns for publishers over the past few weeks.

Zelnick notes that "[the video games] business has been largely immune to piracy" thanks to factors like file size, how console ecosystems work, and aspects related to the online nature of the games industry. That said, Strauss continues, there is a threat posed to the industry because of AI. However, he assures listening investors that Take-Two is appropriately scaling its measures against bad faith actors using artificial intelligence.

"We are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defences and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And - at the same time, without in any way being cavalier - every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy, [and] this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it."

Zelnick pivots back to AI again later in the call, where one investor once again asks about AI, seemingly keen to learn whether the CEO feels it can provide GTA 6 developer Rockstar with any kind of "competitive advantage" in the games industry. Given Zelnick's previous comments on the subject, his answer was not a complete surprise.

"It's always been true [that technology benefits us]," explains Zelnick. "We've always created our entertainment inside computers with technology. All advances have benefited us, and I don't expect that that will change - in fact, I hope it'll accelerate. I think at the same time, what we're known for [at Take-Two] is the desire to make the best entertainment on Earth. And, more often than not, we have succeeded - and the creativity that drives that success is human creativity harnessing technology. And I think that's what you'll see in the future, too.

"Undoubtedly some of the most recent technological advances that you've seen have made it easier to create assets. Where all that is consistent with the story of our business. When I started in interactive entertainment (longer ago than I would like to say), it was really difficult to create an asset in a computer. Today, it's a whole lot easier - but you know what's not easier? Making a big hit. Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future. And hit creation remains the purview of human beings."

This isn't the first instance of AI skepticism we've seen from Strauss Zelnick. Back in March, he outright rejected the idea that AI can tackle games on the scale of GTA 6. Elsewhere in the call, the Take-Two CEO reiterated how well GTA 6 is tracking as he reasserted pre-order numbers are well above expectations, and promised that the success of the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two's gaming business.

#3873. There were 47 graphics chip makers in 1998. Where did they all go?

Suddenly, making faster chips mattered less than a faster release schedule - and most of the industry couldn’t keep up

Some may find this hard to believe, given the absolute state of the market today, but if you were building a gaming PC in 1998, the hard part wasn’t finding somewhere that had 3D cards in stock for a reasonable price. It was choosing the right one among a glut of potential, reasonably affordable options.

In 1998, 47 companies were designing or selling PC graphics, driving a market that hit 130 million units and outsold PCs themselves. Just two years later, at the turn of the new millennium, only 15 remained, and not long after that, there were merely two: Nvidia and ATI, nowadays part of AMD.

But the Nvidia of the late 1990s and early 2000s was a far cry from the vast (if tarnished) juggernaut it is today, and at the time it wasn’t even the obvious survivor. Research firm 4th Wave put ATI top for 1998 with 24.5 million 3D chips sold, followed by S3 with 15.2 million and Intel, in its first year in the market, with 6.5 million. Nvidia came fourth on 6.4 million. 3dfx, the company whose Voodoo cards had made 3D gaming on PC a thing in the first place, sold 5.2 million.

Each of those companies went under or sold up for one reason or another, but what’s striking is how most did so within a few years of one another. In the four years between 1998 and 2002, the graphics business essentially stopped rewarding whoever had the fastest chip, instead favouring the companies that could iterate the fastest. A new chip every six months or so for the same APIs everyone used, backed by enough capital to ride out the dot-com crash. Nvidia was built for that; almost nobody else was.

The first companies to go didn’t need any help from Nvidia, though. 3D acceleration had made the humble graphics chip a much bigger and more expensive thing to design, and plenty of incumbents that had found their footing on 2D couldn’t afford to keep going. Tseng Labs stopped developing graphics chips at the end of 1997 with roughly $28 million still in the bank, selling its graphics engineers to ATI for about $3 million. Rendition, maker of the Vérité V1000 3D accelerator, agreed to sell itself to memory maker Micron in June 1998, and ATI bought Chromatic Research for $67 million that October.

In its prospectus for its January 1999 IPO, Nvidia warned that PC makers brought out new systems as often as twice a year, on a spring and fall schedule, and that missing one was a serious risk. The company subsequently reorganised itself around that schedule, releasing the GeForce 256 in October 1999 and the GeForce 3 in February 2001. By 2002, Nvidia’s annual report disclosed that separate design teams were working on several generations of chips at once.

By this point, though, the writing had been on the wall for quite some time. S3, then the world’s second-largest graphics chip maker, wrote in its annual report for 1999 that a graphics chip stayed on sale for 12 to 18 months, and that a delay "as short as a few months" could cost it a design win with a PC maker. Any company that was rolling out just one major chip per year was launching against a rival’s refresh at best. At worst, it was launching late against next-gen chips.

That’s essentially what happened to 3dfx when Rampage, the chip that was meant to succeed the Voodoo5, never shipped. The company lost its other big advantage around the same time with Glide, its own programming interface that only ran on Voodoo cards. Glide flourished while Direct3D, Microsoft’s rival interface built into Windows, was still lacking features, meaning that plenty of games ran best on 3dfx hardware, but that lead was quickly eroded once Direct3D and rivals’ OpenGL drivers caught up; developers could now write a game once and run it on anyone’s card. By 1999, Creative was selling Nvidia-based Riva TNT cards with drivers that let Glide games run on them. 3dfx sued, then open-sourced Glide altogether that December.

By then, though, 3dfx had already made its most damaging mistake. A year earlier, on December 14, 1998, it agreed to buy graphics card maker STB Systems for about $141 million in stock, and CEO Greg Ballard said the Voodoo3 would only be sold on 3dfx’s cards. That revelation left Diamond and Creative in a tough spot, having built their gaming lines on Voodoo chips. They were now stuck high and dry without access to the new one.

3dfx was solely concerned with its margins here. The price of its single-chip Voodoo Banshee card dropped from $150 to $89 within a month of launch. With prices in freefall, selling the finished Voodoo Banshee meant that 3dfx pocketed the margin that’d otherwise go to a partner like Diamond or Creative. Those boardmakers inevitably walked, and went where the chips were. STB had been selling Nvidia cards right up to the deal, and its last annual report includes a $3 million note it held from "Nvidia Corporation, a supplier." Creative already had Riva TNT cards on shelves, and Nvidia, which then didn’t make its own cards, would sell its chips to anyone.

Intel, meanwhile, was causing problems from the other end of the market. Its i740 "Auburn" graphics chip launched in early 1998, and Microprocessor Report, the newsletter for the industry’s engineers, argued that Intel’s arrival encouraged Cirrus Logic, Oak and others to fold that year. Just over a year later, after lacklustre sales, Intel confirmed that it was ending support for the i740, then pulled out of standalone desktop graphics chips altogether to put graphics into its motherboard chipsets instead, starting with the i810. This was extremely problematic for companies like S3, Trident, and SiS. They survived on cheap chips for big PC makers, and by the second half of 2001, estimates say Intel’s integrated graphics business had risen to control 55% of the market. That, in turn, pushed S3 to sell its graphics business to a VIA joint venture for $323 million.

Then the money ran out. Venture funding for graphics startups had already dried up in 1999 as the dot-com bubble deflated, and exits inevitably followed. 3dfx lost $100.5 million in the second quarter of 2000, with its CEO blaming a late Voodoo5, and on December 15 that year it sold its assets to Nvidia for $70 million in cash (and a million Nvidia shares) after failing to secure credit. STMicroelectronics, which made the PowerVR-based Kyro II, quit PC graphics in early 2002.

ATI, however, survived alongside Nvidia because it was already operating in the way the new market wanted it to. It was the biggest seller at the time, and it made its own graphics cards, which Microprocessor Report said brought in most of its revenue and margin. So, making its own cards wasn’t 3dfx’s mistake; it was locking out boardmakers who had been selling Voodoo cards for it. That pushed those boardmakers towards Nvidia, and a late Voodoo5 and cash crunch dealt the death blow. ATI also used its stock to buy the engineers that its rivals were shedding: Tseng’s, Chromatic’s, then, in February 2000, ArtX’s for $400 million, a team that’d just designed the Flipper graphics chip for Nintendo’s GameCube.

For the next two decades, the the graphics industry was dominated by ATI - which eventually folded into AMD in 2006 - and Nvidia. For a while, it was a real fight. AMD paid $5.4 billion for ATI, and in the second quarter of 2010, Radeon cards briefly overtook Nvidia in discrete graphics shipments. However, AMD had a problem: it couldn’t really afford ATI. It wrote off $1.6 billion of goodwill from the deal about a year after it closed, and its PC chip business kept struggling.

By early 2015, AMD’s CPU and GPU revenue was down 38% on the year, and the company was close to negative book value. Its quarterly R&D budget had fallen to its lowest level since 2004, with Nvidia spending nearly half as much again. Radeon cards stayed on the same Graphics Core Next architecture for about seven years before RDNA arrived in 2019. By then, Nvidia had already launched its RTX cards with dedicated ray tracing hardware and Tensor cores for AI, and it never gave that lead back.

Intel was the only company with pockets deep enough to try breaking back in. Its first go, Larrabee, was cancelled as a consumer graphics chip in December 2009. It finally got there in 2022, when the Arc A770 went on sale from $329, alongside the cheaper A750. Both arrived after repeated delays and struggled with older DirectX 9 games, and many observers - RPS included - put their chances of breaking up the Nvidia-AMD duopoly at low. By the time then-hardware editor James returned to the A750 in 2023, Intel had drastically improved its drivers, bringing big gains to both general performance and DX9 compatibility. Even then, the Arc series had yet to prove it could work well at launch, without the need to be ironed out across months of updates.

The second generation did indeed fare better, with the Arc B580 successfully selling out at $249 in December 2024. But that still barely impacted the wider industry, with Intel sitting at just 1% of graphics card shipments in the third quarter of 2025 and around 2% this spring, when Nvidia took roughly 90% of the 12.5 million cards shipped.

It now looks like Intel is on its way back out of gaming graphics cards. In April, leaker Jaykihn claimed that its next-generation Celestial gaming cards had been cancelled "long ago," and the latest rumours say B580 supply could be cut so Intel can sell more Arc Pro cards for, surprise surprise, AI work. It’s important to note that Intel hasn’t confirmed any of that, and one of its execs has said that Arc isn’t leaving its PC roadmap. Still, Intel had everything 3dfx didn’t: the cash, the PC makers on side, and the same APIs as everyone else. But money can’t buy two decades of Nvidia and AMD fixing their drivers game by game, and it seems to have decided its capital is better spent on AI anyway.

Evidently, the question of where all the other GPU makers went does not have one single answer. Some couldn’t afford the rising costs, some couldn’t keep pace with a new Nvidia chip every six months, and some lost their cheap business to Intel’s integrated graphics or went under when the dot-com bubble burst. Left over was a Nvidia/ATI (later AMD) duopoly, and PC gamers haven’t exactly done well out of it. We saw the RTX 4080 launch at $1,199 in 2022, nearly twice the 3080’s price, and the ongoing, AI-driven RAM shortage has pushed prices higher still.

In 1998, 47 companies wanted your money. Now there are two, and the bigger one, Nvidia, sells nine of every 10 graphics cards - yet still makes most of its money from data centres. Eighteen years on, it's a bad time to be a PC gamer, and nobody’s in a hurry to make things any better.

TSMC, the juggernaut that produces roughly 90% of the world's most advanced chips, has discovered a data leak said to contain over 46,000 employee records, according to Seeking Alpha.

The company made a Form 6-K filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Thursday, stating: "TSMC has found that some of our current and former employee data was made available on an external website without authorization. Currently, we have found no evidence that TSMC’s systems have been compromised."

The company says the info has been verified to match data "stored in the system services of a cloud service provider," although said provider is not named. TSMC says it has informed those impacted by the breach and is providing support, and has also engaged with the cloud service vendor, investigating authorities, and a third-party cybersecurity agency to "ascertain the facts and take necessary actions."

Taiwanese outlet United Daily News reports that hackers were allegedly offering the employee records on an underground forum for the princely sum of three bitcoin, in exchange for 6.9 GB worth of private data.

The outlet also says that, "according to information online" (via machine translation), hackers were also selling what appears to be TSMC employee data on other forums, releasing a small sample which is said to contain a vast array of personal details, including national ID numbers, addresses, and banking information.

TSMC has confirmed in its statement that the leaked data is unrelated to the company's operations, or customer-related information.

This isn't the first time TSMC has been in the headlines in relation to cybersecurity. Back in 2023, ransomware outfit LockBit attempted to extort the company for $70 million after a claimed hack.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

TSMC denied it had been directly hacked, revealing in a statement that IT hardware supplier Kinmax Technology had been the victim of a "cybersecurity incident" instead, which "led to the leak of information pertinent to server initial setup and configuration." Kinmax also released a statement at the time confirming the breach.

Being such a large and wealthy company at the heart of the tech supply chain, it's no surprise that hackers are keen to gain any details on TSMC if they can. In both these cases, it seems that TSMC's own systems remained secure, but an outside party may have let the side down.

Regardless, I doubt it's the last major data leak I'll be writing about before 2026 is out. This year has been characterised by cybersecurity incidents left, right and centre, and in this every-more-interconnected world, it seems even some of the most security-conscious companies are far from immune.

#3871. PS5 QSSR support added to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, CONTROL Resonant, ARC Raiders, THE FINALS, No Man’s Sky, and Hell Let Loose: Vietnam

PlayStation 5‘s Quick Spectral Super Resolution—the base console equivalent of PlayStation 5 Pro’s artificial intelligence upscaling solution PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution—will add Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, CONTROL Resonant, ARC Raiders, THE FINALS, No Man’s Sky, and Hell Let Loose: Vietnam to its lineup of supported titles, Sony Interactive Entertainment announced.

“Having seen great results integrating [Quick Spectral Super Resolution] in Marvel’s Wolverine, our team decided to bring it to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 as well, in an update that’s live now!,” said Insomniac Games head of technology Mike Fitzgerald. “We’re excited for players to swing back into our 2023 title and see [Quick Spectral Super Resolution]’s exciting image stability and sharpness benefits in both Fidelity and Performance modes.”

Remedy Entertainment is bringing Quick Spectral Super Resolution to CONTROL Resonant on PlayStation 5, with noticeable improvements in image stability and fine detail.

“It’s great to see PlayStation bringing the same kind of leap on the PlayStation 5 that [PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution] brought to PlayStation 5 Pro,” said Remedy Entertainment senior graphics programmer Erik Jansson. “[Quick Spectral Super Resolution] gives CONTROL Resonant a much more stable and detailed image, and we’ve worked closely with Sony to have it ready in an update coming in December.”

“With the new [Quick Spectral Super Resolution] coming soon to ARC Raiders and THE FINALS, we can deliver increased sharpness, better environmental clarity and overall visual improvements to even more PlayStation players,” said Embark Studios technical art director Mikael Linderholm. “We are very happy to see Sony’s continued investment in PlayStation technology translate into meaningful improvements for all players, bringing more immersive experiences across the PlayStation ecosystem.”

“No Man’s Sky gives players an infinite procedural universe to explore,” said Hello Games founder Sean Murray. “When every star in the night sky is a real solar system players can visit, we care a great deal about the quality of every pixel.

“The team has always been passionate about pushing the boundaries of technology on PlayStation. [Quick Spectral Super Resolution] allows us to render the universe in sharper, cleaner and more beautiful detail, while delivering the best possible framerate. Look for it in the next few weeks.

“It’s another step towards making the universe of No Man’s Sky even more immersive to explore.”

“We’re delighted to confirm that we are adding [Quick Spectral Super Resolution] to Hell Let Loose: Vietnam on PlayStation 5 through an upcoming update,” said Expression Games game director Paul Rustchynsky. “Console visuals are something our community has been passionate about, and [Quick Spectral Super Resolution] will bring sharper, cleaner image quality to the battlefield, from dense jungle to the chaos of a full-scale firefight. We can’t wait for our PlayStation players to see the difference.”

#3870. Switch 2 and Switch consoles updated to version 23.5.0 as Nintendo quietly re-introduces eShop gifting

Nintendo has just pushed out a new update to all Switch and Switch 2 consoles, bringing the firmware on both up to version 23.5.0. The headline change with the new update is support and compatibility for an upcoming update that will allow members of a Nintendo Account family group to gift games to one another.

The feature itself is expected to go live on 17th November, 2026. "Just in time for the holidays, a new feature will let family group members gift digital games to other members of their group," says a post on a dedicated blog on the Nintendo site. "You will be able to gift digital products that you purchase through Nintendo eShop on your device to family group members. This includes eligible games as well as DLC and upgrade packs. As a reminder, anyone with a Nintendo Account can easily set up a family group and add members (up to 8 total)."

The publisher notes, however, that "some products may not be eligible for digital gifting" and that "supervised accounts are not able to send digital gifts". Additionally, "the number of digital gift purchases allowed in a given period is limited".

"This feature is a great way to celebrate a special occasion with your kids. Happy gifting!" concludes Nintendo. Just in time for the holidays, how thoughtful. It's worth noting that a previous iteration of this support was included back on the Nintendo Wii, but that was much more robust than this - back then, the publisher allowed users to send WiiWare or Virtual Console games to anyone on their Wii Friend list via the Wii Shop Channel, rather than just those limited to their immediate group. This functionality was lost in 2019, alongside the closure of the Wii Shop Channel.

#3869. Minerva Rising is a Frostpunk-meets-Silo underground city builder in which rebel citizens can hack your camera

Minerva Rising is a post-apocalyptic city builder in which your city extends deep underground, divided into levels with their own resources, industries, and communities. You are an artificial intelligence with overall control, but watch out: if you alienate the population of any particular level by, say, forgetting to supply them with oxygen, subversives may rise up and cut your feed, blinding you to their activities.

I'm keen to know whether it's possible for every level to lose faith in you and hack your cameras, reducing the game to a pile of "SIGNAL NOT FOUND" messages. I'm also imagining turning the feeds back on and discovering that everybody is having a massive orgy. Stupid sexy vault dwellers! You'll go forth and multiply when Deep Thought tells you to, and not a second before.

When solo developer Jonny Strellman emailed me about Minerva Rising, he framed it as "Frostpunk meets Silo", Silo being that apparently quite good Apple TV+ show starring Rebecca Ferguson. (I assume if you're reading this, I don't need to introduce you to Frostpunk.) It's got at least one thing neither of those productions has: in-game footage of Steamboat Willy, displayed on propaganda screens you might set up, if you want to buoy cave-dweller morale with thoughts of the copyright-expired world before. Alternatively, you can encourage them to fall in love with the caves themselves, which may harbour luxurious waterfalls and incandescent fungus.

Who needs the sun? Can't get sunburn from a glowing mushroom, can you? Look, citizens of level 13: you'd better overcome your distaste for giant toadstools or I'm turning the power off again. Damn it, you stay the hell away from my factory reset button. "WELCOME TO MICROSOFT WINDOWS 95." Balls! "[✓] SHOW THIS WELCOME SCREEN NEXT TIME YOU START WINDOWS." Right, that's it. I don't appear to have any military options in this game, but I'm pretty sure I can redesignate your whole cave as a compost heap.

"Cut through new strata of earth and ethics each playthrough," the Steam page enthuses. "No two games will be the same. One run might face blight and starvation, while another might be low on coal for producing power. Your decisions and the resources you find provide different challenges each time you play. Even if your people live to see the sun again, there are varied and sundry ways to get there." There's no release date for it yet. If you'd rather build cities in the other direction, check out Stario: Haven Tower.

Jason Ronald – vice president of Xbox's gaming devices and ecosystem team – has spoken in more detail about what Project Helix actually is. Namely, it doesn't sound like it's a Steam Machine.

To celebrate the 25th anniversary since the original Xbox was released and Halo arrived in our lives (and almost 26 since The Rock revealed the console), Microsoft has released a magazine about the platform online. While a lot of it is about the history of the console, some details about the future of Xbox are sprinkled in there, with news about future releases like Fable, and a hint that there's maybe something going on with games like Crash Bandicoot and Tony Hawk. But the most significant bit of info is some more details about what Project Helix is.

Ronald – who Microsoft describes as the vice president of next generation – says "it's really designed to be the ultimate gaming machine – one that removes all the barriers of play that have historically existed," while touting its backwards compatibility capabilities, mentioning that he's "able to bring four generations of my Xbox library and progression with me and have it available instantly."

He also speaks about removing "the arbitrary constraints between console and PC games," while explaining more about what Project Helix's rumored PC connection actually is. "We're very clear on the design goal" Ronald explains, "Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games."

Of course, the real question is how all-encompassing is the PC integration going to be. Presumably the Xbox Store is a sure bet, and probably Battle.net too. But the idea of having your Steam library available on console would be a pretty unassailable win for the console, but sadly I really don't see that happening in the age of Steam Machines.

Xbox Project Helix console could cost as much as $1,800 and is reportedly set to launch by Christmas 2028.

#3867. After being laid off by Microsoft, former Doom devs found new Smash TV-influenced FPS studio that isn't "subject to investor demands"

Their first project: televised deathgame shooter Danger Pay

Back in July, Doom developers id Software laid off around a hundred people as part of wider Microsoft blood-letting. Now, a few of those devs have founded a new employee-owned studio, Hidden Horses. Their first project is Danger Pay, a single-player FPS influenced by ancient arcade blaster Smash TV (pictured) and dystopian movies such as deadly gameshow fable The Running Man – itself an influence on Smash TV.

Hidden Horses have 20 id Software alumni on the books, including former lead VFX artist Todd Boyce, principal engine programmer Dustin Land, senior AI and gameplay engineer Daniel Young, producer Andrew Willis, senior technical designer Jordan Turner, principal technical designer Tim Locke, and senior skybox artist Allison Dombek. They're looking to make "the kind of old school shooters that we think people want more of," in Land's words.

All members of Hidden Horses own a share of the company, with bosses "democratically" appointed, in the words of a FAQ. "Our structure is quite flat, and we elect leaders when needed," Willis told Vertical Slice in a separate interview. "Financially, this means we are not subject to investor demands and the preservation of the company and the jobs it sustains is paramount over needless growth and our 'capital' doesn't compete for returns with other potential investments."

All of which is obviously gesturing towards the horse elephant in the room: Microsoft, who've made enormous cuts to their Xbox biz in their eagerness to further supercharge their $4 trillion market value.

"We've replicated some things, changed some things, and added others [from our id Software days]," Willis went on. "Overall, I think top-down hierarchy is something we all have bad experiences with—we also don't want to trend chase or make a game by focus group. We want to make the kinds of classic gameplay focused games that we would play ourselves. We think there is a market for that and our experiences with the gaming community in our past work history informs that."

Willis's hope is that the "flat" structure will motivate staff to work harder, because they feel like they have a meaningful say over the company's direction. "It allows all ideas to be considered and means we don't miss out on any contributions from our employees just because they don't sit high up in some arbitrary hierarchy," he said..

I'm cynical about "flat" company structures, myself. I think they are very often just an excuse for the biggest egos in a company to throw their weight around. It can work given a friendly initial mix of founders, but it gets complicated when you start hiring new people who don't have the same chemistry. Mind you, there are no plans to expand the company dramatically for the foreseeable. "We want to create a vehicle that allows us to make games for our livelihoods, not to make crazy profits and get 100x returns," Willis went on. I'm also a bit leery of the fact that Hidden Horses have popped up a Kickstarter, because I'm leery about crowd-funding in general, even when Peter Molyneux isn't involved. The studio founders are currently working on some promotional initiatives to drum up support, including a studio documentary and *squints* a promotional beer? Still, I'm happy to hear that at least a few Cacodemon wranglers jettisoned by the big M have landed on their hooves feet. I wish Hidden Horses the best of luck with it all. As for Danger Pay, proper screens, footage and release details are to follow.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Skin distribution seems to be an issue in pretty much any game with more than one hero and clear favourites. Marvel Rivals has come under fire for it for a while now, ever since players got wise to which heroes were favourites and which had clearly been shoved to the side.

It all came to a head a few months ago when the summer skins were released, and it was revealed that Storm was the only female hero to not get a legendary costume among all the swimsuit designs. Players did not look upon this favourably, as Storm is a hugely popular character and had already gone a long time without the same kind of legendary skins as other heroes like Luna Snow and had been passed over for skins in the Disco and Egyptian God skin lines.

But all the player complaints seem to have gotten through to NetEase, with creative director Guangyun Chen acknowledging in a dev diary that "season 10 has been a challenging one for us." Not only were players upset about only one hero being released this season, but the devs have "been closely following the community's feedback regarding certain heroes receiving fewer costumes. With strong demands for more high-quality Legendary costumes featuring recolours and ultimate ability visual upgrades."

The decision has since been made to upgrade Storm's summer skin to legendary tier with the devs "targeting a release around Christmas this December" for it. Other slightly forgotten heroes who will be getting some visual upgrades include Human Torch, who will get a legendary costume in early December which includes "recolours and ultimate ability VFX". Cloak and Dagger will also be getting a (presumably Valentines Day-themed) skin in February.

"We've been hard at work at this for almost eight months," Guangyun Chen says. "Cloak's design will include full legs. We fully re-animated Cloak's entire movement set strictly for this, we really hope you enjoy it."

But with all these new redesigns and costumes on the way, Guangyun Chen wants to remind players that skins can't just be made or changed at a moment's notice: "Please understand that art asset production requires a certain lead time and simply can't be done overnight. Generally, a single costume takes eight to 10 months to produce from start to finish."

Storm's redesigned summer skin has been in the works for three months already, with the finished product coming out after five months of work. That's under the average of eight to 10 months, but this sounds like the exception not the rule.

#3865. Switch 2 US sales soar again thanks to The Legend of Zelda effect, as it enjoys its best week of the year so far

Could a remade Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time be exciting enough to revitalise Switch 2 hardware sales? That was the big question. And early sales figures suggest the answer is yes, it can.

The Switch 2, which had been declining in hardware sales over the last few months, just had its highest (dollar) sales week of 2026 in the US so far following the game's release, according to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella on Bluesky.

The accompanying Legend of Zelda: 40th Anniversary Edition console in particular is responsible for a notable jump in Switch 2 hardware dollar sales. The themed, special edition console has been popular, with various retailers immediately running out of stock and a rise in scalping.

It's worth noting that The Legend of Zelda: 40th Anniversary Edition console, priced $520 / £430, does not include a copy of the game. Also, because the console was released 29th October, and the Ocarina of Time remake on 5th November, their sales results will come in separate monthly reports.

The Ocarina of Time launch also caused US hardware spending to jump by 81 percent during the week ending 31st October compared to the same period last year.

Christian Donlan awarded The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time a glitzy five stars in Eurogamer's review, writing: "This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday."

#3864. "One of those ways where you can use AI ethically": CDPR have modified Geralt's Polish voice in The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past with genAI, due to actor's stroke

Jacek Rozenek reportedly gave his blessing

CD Projekt Red have reportedly enlisted Ukrainian AI firm Respeecher to modify voice lines recorded for the Polish version of Geralt of Rivia in The Witcher 3's upcoming Songs of the Past expansion. The move's been made with the permission of Geralt's Polish voice actor, Jacek Rozenek, and is rooted in the studio wanting his new lines to sound similar to the ones he recorded for the original game prior to having a stroke which has altered how he sounds.

Game File report that after suffering a stroke in 2019 and having to rehabilitate his speech, Rozenek was able to record some lines as Geralt for a quest in The Witcher 3's 2022 next-gen update, but that doing so left the actor "so exhausted". With next year's Songs of the Past expansion, CD Projekt Red were seemingly more concerned about making sure lines recorded by post-stroke Rozenek don't sound markedly different to those he recorded a decade ago for the base game and its existing expansions.

After a meeting between the two sides confirmed that Rozenek's voice had grown lower and gruffer due to some combination of the stroke and him simply getting older, the studio made the decision not to recast the actor, but instead let modify Respeecher modify his lines to make them sound closer to those original recordings. Rozenek reportedly gave his blessing for this to go ahead. "The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago," he told Game File. "I have great trust...for the creators of this game."

This isn't the first time CD Projekt Red have enlisted Respeecher's services. Back in 2023, it was revealed that the studio had used speech synthesis software to make ripperdoc Viktor Vektor's lines in the Polish version of Cyberpunk 2077's Phantom Liberty expansion sound like actor Miłogost Reczek. Reczek died in 2021 before he could reprise his role as Vektor for the DLC, so rather than recasting the character across the whole game to avoid noticeable differences in voice, CD Projekt got another actor to voice Vektor's new lines for Phantom Liberty, then used the genAI tech to make those lines sound like Reczek was delivering them. CD Projekt Red said at the time that they'd gotten permission from Reczek's family before going ahead with their plan.

Speaking to Game File about this latest use of genAI on Rozenek's Songs of the Past lines, CD Projekt localisation producer Mikołaj Szwed noted that "as a person working with voice actors over all the regions in the world, this is a big concern". "I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically, with consent and also to do something good," he added. The argument the studio are making at current is that this was "a special case" due to Rozenek's specific situation with Songs of the Past.

Geralt's English voice actor Doug Cockle reportedly won't have his lines for the new expansion get the same genAI treatment, nor will any lines Rozenek records for future Witcher games, with the studio seemingly happy to lean on the passage of in-game time as an explanation for Geralt sounding different in the latter case.

As ever, there's a debate to be had as to whether CD Projekt Red should have simply recast Rozenek's role in Songs of the Past if the difference bothered them so, possibly while bringing the actor on to help tutor whomever his human replacement for Songs of the Past would be in nailing the exact gravelly tone needed for Geralt. That way, you'd have two actors being paid for work rather than forking out for genAI instead of one of them, though it's possibly an idea that'd only work well in theory. If I were Rozenek I'm not sure I'd be totally happy aiding someone who could potentially be tapped to replace me going forwards, though it does very much seem like the lesser of two evils when compared to the potential of voice actors being replaced by genAI line readings.

As far as the game alone is concerned, I'm also not sure Geralt's voice being different in the new expansion is something that'd bother me too much when playing. One would assume he'd not suddenly be sounding like a member of Alvin and the Chipmunks, and there are plenty of storyline justifications you could concoct or lean on for him sounding that bit gruffer at times.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has been out for just over a week, and player stats prove that I'm not the only one who's died a few too many times to a ReDead. Solidarity.

If you've not been using the Zelda Notes app while playing the Ocarina of Time remake, this is your sign to start. Found within the Nintendo Switch App, its compatibility with the new remake is incredible if you're keen to track down all the secrets available, with an interactive map showing your completion in each area, if you're missing any Gold Skulltalas or Pieces of Heart, and more. Even if you want to go through the remake without a guide, though, it's still worth it just to have a peek at your player stats and see how they compare to everyone else's.

As highlighted by GoNintendo, the first week or so of Ocarina of Time remake stats in Zelda Notes' Global Play Data section are pretty interesting. Skulltalas are the most commonly defeated enemy, while the ever-horrifying ReDead and Gibdos are responsible for 18% of all deaths in the remake. I can't say that's surprising – they've always been a pain to deal with (as well as being utterly terrifying), but now we just have the stats to prove it.

Amusingly, tied with the hard-hitting Iron Knuckles for 7% of all deaths each, the runner-up here is, simply, fire. Sounds like a few too many people got overconfident when exploring Death Mountain without the Goron tunic. Please, stop setting poor Link on fire, folks.

A lot of stats here are still obviously being influenced by the enormous number of people who are only just diving into the game. Most people, for example, have only traveled around 1 kilometer in Hyrule, as opposed to a much smaller number who've already passed 200km. Some stats are more indicative of a longer playtime, though – the majority of folks are apparently professional gardeners, with over 1,000 pieces of grass cut, and 40% of people's most-used form of magic being the Lenses of Truth is almost certainly thanks to the group who've been through the Shadow Temple already.

The Zelda Notes app also tracks your time to clear the game – at 26 hours, I fall into the "20 hours+" category, which is the most common result, but some folks were very quick, coming in at just over 10 hours, instead.

If there's one thing these stats prove though, it's that more of you need to go fishing. The average, by quite a margin, is just one to four fish caught – we've got to get those numbers up. Now, if only the app could somehow track how many people got stuck in the Water Temple, too.

#3861. Amid soaring PC hardware prices, gaming monitors are getting cheaper and cheaper. Here's why, and what to buy

Hello, good local-time-zone-adjusted afternoon, and let's just say it's been a while. But I come back to you now at the turn of the technological tide. Well, sort of. Sadly I'm not here to predict an end to the ridiculous AI-fuelled chip crisis. That whole mess has a couple of years to run, surely.

Instead I speak of screens, where there is actually some very good news. In short, have you seen how cheap PC gaming monitors are? I mean remarkably, almost stupendously, cheap. I'm talking £60 / $60 for an entry-level 1080p panel with triple-digit refresh rate, sub-£200 / $250 for high-refresh 4K gaming. Heck, even OLED monitors now start with a "2" in both currencies.

Also bear in mind we've had a fair old bit of inflation in recent years. A 4K panel bought today for £200 is equivalent to paying roughly £150 back in 2020. All the while, that same £200 / $200 right now won't buy you a current-model gaming graphics card at all, even the most feeble example, and will barely secure a basic dual-channel 16GB DDR5 memory kit. Youch.

So, I think we can all agree monitors are cheap in the current chip-catastrophe context. The immediate question is why? The answer isn't all that complicated, actually. Most obviously, the display market isn't being devoured by the AI craze. All those data centres are stuffed with GPUs, memory chips and NAND flash, not monitors.

By way of example, one of the largest new AI data centres on Earth is Microsoft's new Fairwater site in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin. It's thought to pack hundreds of thousands of Nvidia Blackwell GPUs. The cost doesn't bear thinking about, but those GPUs are built into what's known as "headless" server racks. In other words, they have no screens at all. Ultimately, the key compute hardware is all managed remotely, in which capacity the Fairwater facility is reported to currently have around 375 employees. If we generously assume each has two PC monitors, that's only 750 for the entire site.

AI isn't really driving demand on the end-user side of the equation, either. Put it this way: you don't need to buy a new phone, laptop or PC to access the latest models. At the same time, the display market is suffering from something of a glut of overcapacity. Chinese companies built out huge capacity in LCD panel manufacturing over the past decade, to the extent factories are now running underutilised. Meanwhile, even the OLED market is arguably oversupplied.

In fact, Samsung and LG, the two big noises in large OLED panel manufacturing (as opposed to OLED displays for tablets and phones), have been shifting emphasis away from TV panels to PC monitors because the latter offer better margins. Meanwhile, the AI boom has almost definitely meant lower demand for new PCs. Certainly, the big research houses point to cratering PC sales thanks to higher component costs. Long story short, that's oodles of capacity combined with weakening demand. Like I said, the explanation for cheap monitors isn't exactly rocket surgery, if you know what I mean.

What is a bit more complicated is making sense of what's available today in the gaming monitor market. With so much choice, where exactly is the very best value to be found? And are there any remaining pain points?

Monitor specifications, to be sure, can be tricksy at the best of times. But if you're looking for some blanket rules to fling casually over the whole LCD monitor market - I'll be digging deeper into OLED tech another day - try these for size. Look for, at minimum, 300 nits brightness and 1ms response times. Refresh rates are a slightly more complicated call, but for the vast majority of games, 144Hz is plenty. For "esports-grade multiplayer fare like Counter-Strike or Dota 2, or I think a refresh in the high 200s will get the job done for most. If you'll benefit from more than that, you almost certainly know who you are already.

Oh, and heavily favour IPS over VA panels. Exceptions exist: there are some decent "Rapid VA" panels these days and Samsung, in particular, does some nippy VA models. But a lot of the cheaper stuff is pretty slow and smeary, making VA a risky buy. Finally, don't worry too much about claimed HDR capability, save for the fact that HDR 400 certification at least means the monitor can do 400 nits. Unless a monitor has local dimming, it won't be truly HDR capable.

Anywho, one immediate and rather ironic issue is the growing mismatch between monitors and GPUs. For sure, it's great you can grab a high-refresh 4K monitor for such little money. It's almost hard to believe that you can have this 27-inch IPS MSI for sub-£200 (you're looking at $250 for the same model in the US), and it even has a 288Hz 1080p dual mode.

I actually favour 32 inches with my 4K gaming, and that's naturally a little pricier, especially if you insist on an IPS - which again, you probably should. But even $350 for that kind of panel (here's a comparable model for £340 in the UK) is a fraction of what you'd have paid for a similarly specced model a few years ago. And it probably wouldn't have included dual-mode functionality.

Here's the problem, though. How are you going to drive the thing, what with its eight million-plus pixels? After all, the cheapest RTX 5090 on Newegg right now is over $6,500. So high-end Nvidia GPUs now cost about as much as a decent used car.

Of course, you might be surprised just how effective the likes of an AMD RX 9070 XT or Nvidia RTX 5070-class GPU is at 4K thanks to upscaling technologies including DLSS and FSR. The latest transformer model upscalers really do knock out pretty stellar image quality. Add in a bit of frame gen and you have a compelling combination of visual sharpness, reasonably low latency and nice smoothframe rates, even in the most demanding of games. Perhaps the one thing you can't do is enable full path tracing in a game like Cyberpunk 2077 and still expect a slick experience, but standard ray tracing remains an option.

The bigger snag, unsurprisingly, is that you can no longer bag a 5070 at (let alone below) its original £539 / $549 MSRP. Instead, you're looking at the thick end of £800 / $900. That's a bit of an ask for pairing with a £200 monitor, isn't it?

I'd therefore argue that, for pure gaming purposes, the bang-for-buck sweet spot remains just where it's been sat twiddling its thumbs for the better part of a decade, namely 1440p. That applies to both its vanilla 16:9 aspect variety and my personally preferred ultrawide format, the latter being so very immersive and also pretty nifty for daily multi-tasking. Indeed, the 27-inch 1440p segment even brings the vibrant colours and infinite contrast of OLED panels into a reasonably affordable window.

By way of example, £179 (or $150) is enough for a circa 200Hz, IPS 1440p panel with super low (by IPS standards) pixel response, even if the 250-nit brightness is lower than I'd like. Meanwhile, as I write these words, pricing for big-brand 27-inch 1440p gaming OLEDs kicks off at about £290 in the UK and roughly $270 in the US. Admittedly, those entry-level OLEDs come with some compromises, which I'll cover in a forthcoming post. But what you might call 'proper' OLED panels can be had around the low £300 / $300 mark - not throw-away money, for sure, but relatively accessible.

The 34-inch 1440p ultrawide segment is a bit trickier, however. The good news is that conventional LCD models can be had for relative peanuts, with prices starting at about £220 or $249 for game-focused, high-refresh models. But those two example both use a VA panel, which usually means inferior pixel response.

IPS models are a little thin on the ground when it comes to 34-inch ultrawide, but sneaking in below £300 / $300 is generally possible. The real bummer is OLED, where going ultrawide invokes a massive premium. The best price I can find on a big-brand 34-inch ultrawide today is $629 for this Asus model in the US and £648 for this MSI option in the UK.

That's awfully toppy, especially when you consider that you can grab a 49-inch, 5,120x1,440 ultrawide OLED for barely any more money. I do actually quite like those 49-inch ultrawides, but I have to concede the ergonomics are challenging. However, 4K OLEDs in 27-inch and 32-inch formats can also be had for as much as £100 / $100 less than the current cheapest 34-inch 1440p ultrawides, which doesn't make much sense to me.

Again, with 4K, there's the challenge of keeping all those pixels updated. If you already have a sufficiently mighty graphics card, though, I a 32-inch 4K OLED can make a fantastic all-round option, and something like this MSI model for £549 would be absolutely lovely. You get good pixel density and lots of space for daily desktopping, plus OLED visuals and a large enough panel to be really get you into your games.

It's just a pity that 34-inch OLED ultrawides remain so weirdly expensive, it being a format that ticks so many different boxes. As for my own personal money-no-object pick, well, I'm typing these words on the new Alienware AW3926QW, the 39-inch 5K2K beast with a Tandem WOLED panel and RGB subpixels.

One could argue it's a relative steal at £1,079 or $1,100. I mean, it's pretty much peak current PC gaming display technology, and it's about half the price of what Nvidia's second-tier RTX 5080 graphics card is going for lately. Assuming you can even find one in stock.

At this point, the one major category I haven't covered is LCD monitors with mini-LED full-array local dimming. Cards on the table, I'm not a huge fan of mini-LED monitors. The detailed reasons for that are, perhaps, the subject for another day. But I've reviewed countless models and have yet to see one that didn't come with pretty serious compromises.

That said, the technology has gotten a lot more accessible in the last 12 to 18 months, to the extent that 27-inch 1440p models start at just over $250. I've had that specific model in and came away pretty impressed. It's very, very punchy, and even factoring in the limitations of mini-LED versus OLED when it comes to lighting control and speed, I cannot deny the temptation.

Just for completeness, one further exception to the general rule of cheap gaming monitors involves ultra-high refresh monitors aimed at serious esports aficionados. I'm talking about panels like this 1,000Hz LG I sampled elsewhere. At £800 / $1,000 for a 25-inch 1080p IPS panel it's inevitably a niche proposition, and poor value by normal standards.

I think a much better compromise for just about everyone, short of an actual esports pro, is to grab a larger, higher resolution monitor that offers one of those windowed 1080p modes running at about 500Hz or thereabouts. That way you've got a nice high-res panel for both work and play, as well as that ultra-low latency mode for when you want to dance around Dust 2 doling out the headshots or whatever.

Incidentally, I realise I've gone in a bit hot and heavy with the OLED content here, the implicit assumption being OLED is all that, and notably without addressing the obvious objections like the risk of burn-in. But all that, I hope you'll be pleased to hear, is very much the subject for my next RPS post on all things OLED.

Until then, all I can say is thank goodness PC monitors provide relative respite from the parlous state of much of the rest of the PC component market. It's absolutely brutal out there if you're building a gaming PC, but at least you'll get a lot of screen for your money.

Just to round things out, if anyone has any specific queries at any given price point, form factor or panel type, shout out below and I'll try to steer you in the direction of a decent model.
